lessons.title: Separate MIDI events from audio
lessons.summary: Keep a distinct path for MIDI instructions and for the sound the synth creates.
lessons.body:
Product details in this unit refer to the original Digitakt OS 1.53 manual and Digitakt II OS 1.17 manual, fetched on 16 October 2026. Confirm your model, firmware and current manual before wiring or configuring it.

MIDI (Musical Instrument Digital Interface) lets a sequencer such as a Digitakt tell your synth what to play. These lessons concentrate on MIDI 1.0 performance messages and the separate audio signal route.

The most important idea in this lesson is also the simplest: **MIDI note events do not carry live audio.** MIDI also supports specialised SysEx transfers, including sample data, but that is distinct from an audio stream. It carries short messages such as "key 60 went down on channel 1, quite hard" and "key 60 came back up". The receiving instrument decides what those events sound like.

## Events, not audio

Think of MIDI as a pianist's instructions written down at the moment they happen, not a recording of the piano.

| | MIDI | Audio |
|---|---|---|
| Carries | Performance events here | Audio waveform |
| Size | Often 2–3 MIDI 1.0 bytes | For example 48,000 digital samples/s |
| Sound depends on | Receiver's synthesis | Recorded waveform and playback chain |
| Cable | MIDI (DIN, TRS, USB) | Audio jack, USB audio |

This has practical consequences for your build:

- Your synth needs **two separate paths**: MIDI in (what to play) and audio out (the sound it makes). Connecting the Digitakt's MIDI OUT to your synth does nothing audible until your synth's audio output reaches a mixer or interface.
- A recorded MIDI part in Ableton is a list of events. Change the synth patch and the "recording" sounds different. A recorded audio part is fixed.
- A complete MIDI 1.0 Note On uses three bytes before transport framing. Digital audio storage depends on duration, sample rate, channel count and sample representation; it is usually far larger than the event list.

## Key takeaways
- Keep a distinct path for MIDI instructions and for the sound the synth creates.

questions.prompt: Your Digitakt's MIDI OUT is connected to your synth's MIDI IN, and a MIDI track plays a four-note pattern. What is actually travelling down the MIDI cable?

options.text: A low-resolution copy of the Digitakt's audio, which the synth re-synthesises
options.explanation: These Note On/Off messages do not carry the sound waveform. MIDI can transfer sample data through specialised SysEx protocols, but that is different from the live audio path in this example.

options.text: Short event messages such as note on and note off, each a few bytes long
options.explanation: Correct. MIDI describes performance events (key 60 down at velocity 100, key 60 up). The receiving synth decides what those events sound like.

options.text: A control voltage that sets the synth's pitch directly
options.explanation: That describes analogue CV/gate, a different system. MIDI is a serial digital protocol carrying bytes, not a pitch voltage.

options.text: Both audio and note data multiplexed together, so no separate audio cable is needed
options.explanation: DIN MIDI has no audio at all. You still need an audio cable from the synth's output to your interface or mixer. (USB audio is a separate class from USB MIDI, and DIN carries neither audio nor power.)

questions.workedExample:
1. Ask what the receiver needs in order to play a note: which key, how hard, and when it starts and stops.
2. MIDI encodes exactly those facts as messages, for example `90 3C 64` (note on, channel 1, key 60, velocity 100).
3. The sound is created inside the synth by its oscillators, filters and envelopes.
4. So there are two independent paths to check when something is silent: the MIDI path (are events arriving?) and the audio path (is the synth's output reaching the interface?).

lessons.title: Calculate DIN MIDI transmission time
lessons.summary: Count start and stop bits as well as data: a back-to-back three-byte DIN message takes 0.96 ms.
lessons.body:
## The serial link

Classic MIDI 1.0 runs over a 5-pin DIN cable as an asynchronous serial link. The MIDI electrical specification fixes the format:

- **31,250 bits per second** (±1%).
- Each byte is framed as **1 start bit, 8 data bits, 1 stop bit**, no parity (often written 8-N-1).
- So each byte costs 10 bit-times, which works out at **320 µs** (calculated below).
- Bytes are sent least significant bit first.

How long does one byte take on the wire? Divide the number of bits in its frame by the number of bits the link sends each second. You use this whenever you need to know how quickly MIDI can deliver something.

```formula
t_byte = N_bits / R
t_byte = 10 bit / (31250 bit/s)
t_byte = 0.00032 s = 320 µs
where
t_byte: the time one framed byte occupies the cable, in seconds (s)
N_bits: the number of bits in one frame: 1 start bit + 8 data bits + 1 stop bit = 10 bits
R: the bit rate (baud rate) of the link, in bits per second (bit/s); 31,250 bit/s for DIN MIDI
bit: one binary digit, 0 or 1
s: seconds
µs: microseconds, millionths of a second (1 µs = 0.000001 s)
In words: one MIDI byte takes ten bit-times, and at 31,250 bits per second that is 320 millionths of a second.
```

A whole message is just its bytes sent one after another, so its time is the byte count times the DIN framed-byte duration:

```formula
t_msg = n t_byte
t_msg = 3 × 320 µs
t_msg = 960 µs ≈ 0.96 ms
where
t_msg: the time a complete message occupies the cable, in microseconds (µs) or milliseconds (ms)
n: the number of bytes in the message; 3 for a Note On (status byte plus two data bytes)
t_byte: the time per byte, 320 µs on DIN MIDI
µs: microseconds, millionths of a second
ms: milliseconds, thousandths of a second (1 ms = 1000 µs)
≈: approximately equal to
In words: a three-byte message takes just under one millisecond to send.
```

So a three-byte message takes about **0.96 ms**, roughly a millisecond. That figure matters later when we talk about chords and latency: ten three-byte notes "at once" are actually 30 bytes, about 9.6 ms of wire time, so they are spread over roughly 10 ms. This assumes the bytes are sent back to back with no gaps; a slower sender only makes it longer.

Your microcontroller's UART (universal asynchronous receiver-transmitter) does this framing for you. You configure it for 31,250 baud, 8-N-1, and it hands you whole bytes.

## Key takeaways
- Count start and stop bits as well as data: a back-to-back three-byte DIN message takes 0.96 ms.

## Further reading
- [MIDI 1.0 Detailed Specification 4.2.1 (archived copy at CCRMA)](https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~esteban/teaching/McGill_MUMT306/M1_v4-2-1_MIDI_1-0_Detailed_Specification_96-1-4.pdf)

questions.prompt: How long does a complete three-byte Note On message take to send over DIN MIDI?

options.text: About 0.77 ms
options.explanation: That is 24 bits ÷ 31,250. It forgets the start and stop bits: each byte is framed as 10 bits on the wire.

options.text: About 0.10 ms
options.explanation: This would need a link about ten times faster. DIN MIDI runs at only 31,250 bit/s.

options.text: About 0.96 ms
options.explanation: Correct. Three framed bytes contain thirty bits, giving about 0.96 ms at the nominal DIN MIDI bit rate.

options.text: Exactly 1/31,250 s, because the whole message is sent in parallel
options.explanation: MIDI is serial: one bit at a time. 1/31,250 s is the duration of a single bit.

questions.workedExample:
1. Baud rate: 31,250 bit/s (MIDI electrical specification).
2. Framing: 1 start bit + 8 data bits + 1 stop bit = 10 bits per byte.
3. Total time = bits on the wire ÷ bit rate:

```formula
t = (n N_bits) / R
t = 3 × 10 bit / (31250 bit/s)
t = 30 bit / (31250 bit/s)
t = 0.00096 s ≈ 0.96 ms
where
t: the time to send the whole message, in seconds (s) or milliseconds (ms)
n: the number of bytes in the message; 3 for a Note On
N_bits: bits per framed byte: 1 start + 8 data + 1 stop = 10
R: the DIN MIDI bit rate, 31,250 bits per second (bit/s)
bit: one binary digit
s: seconds
ms: milliseconds, thousandths of a second
≈: approximately equal to
In words: three bytes are 30 bits on the wire, and at 31,250 bits per second they take just under a millisecond.
```

So DIN MIDI can carry only about 1,000 three-byte messages per second, which is why dense data (lots of CCs plus notes) can delay notes.

questions.prompt: A sequencer sends a 10-note chord over DIN MIDI as ten complete three-byte Note On messages, all scheduled for the same instant. Roughly how far apart in time do the first and last notes start?

options.text: 0 ms: messages scheduled together arrive together
options.explanation: DIN MIDI is a single serial line; only one byte can be on the wire at a time.

options.text: About 0.3 ms
options.explanation: That is the time for just one byte, not ten messages.

options.text: About 8.6 ms
options.explanation: Correct. The last message finishes 10 × 0.96 = 9.6 ms after the first begins; the first note can start after 0.96 ms, so the gap between first and last note starts is 9 × 0.96 ≈ 8.6 ms.

options.text: About 96 ms
options.explanation: That is ten times too long: each three-byte message takes about 0.96 ms, not 9.6 ms.

questions.workedExample:
1. One three-byte message is 30 bits; at 31,250 bit/s that takes 0.96 ms.
2. The first note can start when its message completes, at 0.96 ms.
3. The tenth message completes at 9.6 ms.
4. Spread between the first and last starts:

```formula
Δt = (k − 1)t_msg
Δt = (10 − 1) × 0.96 ms
Δt = 8.64 ms ≈ 8.6 ms
where
Δt: the gap between the first note starting and the last note starting, in milliseconds (ms); Δ (delta) means "difference"
k: the number of messages in the chord; 10 here
t_msg: the time to send one three-byte message on DIN, 0.96 ms
ms: milliseconds, thousandths of a second
≈: approximately equal to
In words: the last of ten notes starts nine message-times after the first, about 8.6 ms later.
```

That can be audible on tight material. Running status (next lesson) shortens it by dropping repeated status bytes, and USB MIDI is much faster.

lessons.title: Recognise status and data bytes
lessons.summary: The top bit distinguishes status from seven-bit data; discard orphan data and preserve interrupted messages around MIDI real-time bytes.
lessons.body:
## Status bytes and data bytes

Every MIDI 1.0 byte is one of two kinds, and you can tell which by looking at the top bit:

```
bit:   7 6 5 4 3 2 1 0
status 1 t t t c c c c   0x80-0xFF
data   0 v v v v v v v   0x00-0x7F
```

- A **status byte** has bit 7 set. It says what kind of message this is. For channel messages, the top four bits (`tttt` above, including the 1) are the message type and the bottom four (`cccc`) are the channel.
- A **data byte** has bit 7 clear, so it carries a value from **0 to 127** (7 bits).

Why 128 values? Each extra bit doubles the number of patterns, so the count of distinct values is 2 raised to the number of bits:

```formula
N = 2^b
N = 2^7 = 128
where
N: the number of distinct values the bits can represent (here 0 to 127)
b: the number of bits available for the value; 7 in a MIDI data byte, because bit 7 is reserved
In words: seven free bits give 128 possible values, numbered 0 to 127.
```

With all 8 bits the same formula would give 256 values (0–255); spending one bit on the status/data flag halves that to 128.

This one-bit rule is what makes MIDI robust. If a receiver joins mid-stream or loses a byte, a status byte outside the MIDI real-time class supplies a new message boundary. Real-time bytes also have bit 7 set but may interleave with a message without resetting it. It is also why MIDI values run 0–127 rather than 0–255: the eighth bit is spent on telling status from data.

Channel messages have one or two data bytes according to their status, and a receiver waits for that complete message before dispatching it. System messages differ: some have no data bytes, while SysEx has variable length. It also says receivers should ignore data bytes that are not preceded by a valid status byte, apart from one shortcut called running status, which the later running-status unit covers.

## Key takeaways
- The top bit distinguishes status from seven-bit data; discard orphan data and preserve interrupted messages around MIDI real-time bytes.

## Further reading
- [MIDI 1.0 Detailed Specification 4.2.1 (archived copy at CCRMA)](https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~esteban/teaching/McGill_MUMT306/M1_v4-2-1_MIDI_1-0_Detailed_Specification_96-1-4.pdf)
- [Summary of MIDI 1.0 Messages — MIDI Association](https://midi.org/summary-of-midi-1-0-messages)
- [MIDI 1.0 Electrical Specification Update CA-033 (2014) — MIDI Association](https://www.midi.org/wp-content/uploads/wpforo/default_attachments/1709416667-ca33-MIDI-10-Electrical-Specification-Update.pdf)
- [MIDI tuning standard — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MIDI_tuning_standard)
- [Live 12 manual: Editing MIDI — Ableton](https://www.ableton.com/en/live-manual/12/editing-midi/)
- [Digitakt user manual (OS 1.53; MIDI track note range) — Elektron](https://www.elektron.se/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Digitakt-User-Manual_ENG_OS1.53_260909.pdf)

questions.prompt: Which of these bytes are **status bytes** in MIDI 1.0? Select all that apply.

options.explanation: Correct. Bit 7 is set (1001 0000), so it is a status byte: Note On, channel 1.
Bit 7 is clear (0111 1111), so this is a data byte with value 127, the largest possible data value.
Correct. Bit 7 is set. 0xF8 is the Timing Clock MIDI real-time status byte.
Bit 7 is clear (0011 1100), so this is a data byte, value 60 (often a key number for middle C).

questions.workedExample:
The rule is a single bit test: status bytes have the most significant bit set, data bytes have it clear.

```
0x90 = 1001 0000 -> status
0x7F = 0111 1111 -> data (127)
0xF8 = 1111 1000 -> status
0x3C = 0011 1100 -> data (60)
```

Equivalently, anything from 0x80 to 0xFF is a status byte and anything from 0x00 to 0x7F is data. This is why every MIDI 1.0 data value is limited to 0–127.

questions.prompt: Why are MIDI 1.0 data values limited to 0–127 rather than 0–255?

options.text: Because the UART only sends 7 data bits per frame
options.explanation: The MIDI UART sends 8 data bits per byte (8-N-1). The limit comes from how those bits are used.

options.text: Because 128 velocity levels are all the human ear can distinguish
options.explanation: The limit isn't perceptual; it follows from the byte format. Controllers that need more resolution use 14-bit pairs.

options.text: Because values above 127 are reserved for SysEx data
options.explanation: SysEx data bytes are also 0–127. Values 0x80 and above are always status bytes, including F0/F7.

options.text: Because bit 7 of every byte marks it as status (1) or data (0), leaving 7 bits for a data value
options.explanation: Correct. The top bit distinguishes status from data. A channel or System Common status establishes a new message boundary; MIDI real-time bytes may interleave without replacing the partial message.

questions.workedExample:
1. Each MIDI byte has 8 bits.
2. The format spends the most significant bit to say what kind of byte it is: 1 = status, 0 = data.
3. That leaves 7 bits for a data value:

```formula
N = 2^b
N = 2^7 = 128
where
N: the number of distinct values the bits can hold
b: the number of bits available for the value; 7 here
In words: each bit doubles the number of patterns, so 7 bits give 128 values, numbered 0 to 127.
```

4. The payoff is robustness: if bytes are lost or a device connects mid-stream, a status byte outside the MIDI real-time class establishes a new message boundary. These one-byte statuses can arrive inside an unfinished message and must preserve its parser state.
5. Where 128 steps are too coarse, MIDI combines two data bytes (14 bits: pitch bend, CC MIDI MSB/MIDI LSB pairs), covered in the next lesson.

questions.prompt: You plug your synth into a running sequencer and the first bytes it sees are `3C 64 90 40 7F`. Nothing was received earlier. What should a specification-compliant receiver do?

options.text: Discard `3C 64`, then play key 64 at velocity 127 on channel 1
options.explanation: Correct. Data bytes not preceded by a valid status byte are ignored; `90 40 7F` is a complete Note On.

options.text: Play key 60 at velocity 100, then key 64 at velocity 127
options.explanation: Without a preceding status byte, the receiver doesn't know what `3C 64` means. The spec says to ignore such data bytes.

options.text: Treat `3C` as a status byte because it is the first byte received
options.explanation: 0x3C has bit 7 clear, so it can never be a status byte, whatever its position.

options.text: Reset the parser and ignore everything until a System Reset (FF) arrives
options.explanation: Too drastic. The receiver resynchronises at the very next status byte, 0x90.

questions.workedExample:
1. `3C`: bit 7 clear, a data byte. No status has been received yet, so there is no context. Ignore.
2. `64`: also data, also ignored.
3. `90`: status byte, Note On, channel 1. Now the parser expects two data bytes.
4. `40 7F`: key 64, velocity 127. The message is complete, so start the note.

The spec: "Receivers should ignore Data bytes which have not been properly preceded by a valid Status byte" (except under running status, which needs a status byte to have been seen at some point).

lessons.title: Encode the MIDI channel
lessons.summary: Convert displayed channels to a zero-based low nibble when sending, and add one when displaying received channels.
lessons.body:
Product details in this unit refer to the original Digitakt OS 1.53 manual and Digitakt II OS 1.17 manual, fetched on 16 October 2026. Confirm your model, firmware and current manual before wiring or configuring it.

## Channels

MIDI 1.0 has **16 channels**. They let one cable address up to 16 independent instruments (or parts of a multitimbral instrument). Each receiver is set to listen on one channel (or all of them, "omni") and ignores channel messages for others.

The channel is in the low nibble of the status byte, numbered 0–15 on the wire. People and manuals number them 1–16. To build a channel message's status byte, take the message type's base value (whose low nibble is 0) and put the wire channel number into that empty low nibble:

```formula
S = T + (ch − 1)
S = 0x90 + (10 − 1)
S = 0x90 + 0x09 = 0x99
where
S: the status byte that goes on the wire, written in hexadecimal (0x…)
T: the message type's base value, with its low nibble zero: 0x80 Note Off, 0x90 Note On, 0xB0 Control Change
ch: the channel as people and manuals number it, 1 to 16; subtracting 1 gives the 0–15 wire number
0x: prefix meaning the digits that follow are hexadecimal (base 16), so 0x99 is 153 in decimal
In words: the status byte is the message type in the top nibble and the channel minus one in the bottom nibble; a Note On on channel 10 is 0x99.
```

This off-by-one causes real bugs:

```
user channel  1  -> nibble 0x0
user channel 10  -> nibble 0x9
user channel 16  -> nibble 0xF
```

> [!warning] Channel 1 is 0 on the wire
> When the Digitakt's MIDI track is set to CHAN 1, your synth will see status bytes with channel nibble 0 (for example `0x90` for a note on), not nibble 1 (`0x91`). Store channels internally as 0–15 and add 1 only when displaying them.

## Key takeaways
- Convert displayed channels to a zero-based low nibble when sending, and add one when displaying received channels.

## Further reading
- [MIDI 1.0 Detailed Specification 4.2.1 (archived copy at CCRMA)](https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~esteban/teaching/McGill_MUMT306/M1_v4-2-1_MIDI_1-0_Detailed_Specification_96-1-4.pdf)
- [Summary of MIDI 1.0 Messages — MIDI Association](https://midi.org/summary-of-midi-1-0-messages)
- [MIDI 1.0 Electrical Specification Update CA-033 (2014) — MIDI Association](https://www.midi.org/wp-content/uploads/wpforo/default_attachments/1709416667-ca33-MIDI-10-Electrical-Specification-Update.pdf)
- [MIDI tuning standard — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MIDI_tuning_standard)
- [Live 12 manual: Editing MIDI — Ableton](https://www.ableton.com/en/live-manual/12/editing-midi/)
- [Digitakt user manual (OS 1.53; MIDI track note range) — Elektron](https://www.elektron.se/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Digitakt-User-Manual_ENG_OS1.53_260909.pdf)

questions.prompt: A drum part is sent on MIDI channel 10 (as the user sees it). What is the status byte of a Note On for that channel?

options.explanation: 0xA is 10 in hex, but the wire numbers channels 0–15. Channel 10 is nibble 9, so 0x9A would be channel 11.
0x90 is Note On on channel 1. The channel must be encoded in the low nibble.
0x8n is Note Off, not Note On, and nibble A is channel 11.
Correct. Note On is 0x9n and channel 10 is nibble 10 − 1 = 9, giving 0x99.

questions.workedExample:
1. Note On has the high nibble 9 (binary 1001).
2. Users number channels 1–16; the status byte numbers them 0–15. So channel 10 becomes 10 − 1 = 9.
3. Combine using Python’s bitwise OR: `0x90 | 9` gives `0x99`.

```formula
S = T | (ch − 1)
S = 0x90 | (10 − 1)
S = 0x90 | 0x09 = 0x99
where
S: the status byte sent on the wire, in hexadecimal
T: the message type's base value with an empty low nibble; 0x90 for Note On
ch: the channel as users number it, 1 to 16; here 10
|: bitwise OR; because T's low nibble is all zeros, it just drops the channel number into that nibble (the same as adding)
0x: prefix meaning hexadecimal (base 16); 0x99 is 153 in decimal
In words: put the Note On type in the top nibble and channel 10 minus one (9) in the bottom nibble, giving 0x99.
```

This off-by-one is one of the most common reasons a home-built synth "doesn't respond".

questions.prompt: Your synth is set to receive on MIDI channel 2 (not omni). Which of these status bytes start messages it should act on? Select all that apply.

options.explanation: Correct. Note On (9) with nibble 1, which is channel 2.
Nibble 2 is channel 3. A channel-2 receiver should ignore it.
Correct. Note Off (8) with nibble 1: channel 2.
Correct. Control Change (B) with nibble 1: channel 2.
Nibble 0 is channel 1.

questions.workedExample:
1. Convert the channel to its wire nibble:

```formula
c = ch − 1
c = 2 − 1 = 1
where
c: the channel nibble in the status byte, 0 to 15
ch: the channel as users number it, 1 to 16; here 2
In words: channel 2 is nibble 1 on the wire.
```

2. Any channel message whose low nibble is 1 is for this receiver: `0x81`, `0x91`, `0xB1` all qualify.
3. `0x92` (channel 3) and `0x90` (channel 1) are for other receivers.

```
0x91: 9 Note On,  1 -> ch2  yes
0x92: 9 Note On,  2 -> ch3  no
0x81: 8 Note Off, 1 -> ch2  yes
0xB1: B CC,       1 -> ch2  yes
0x90: 9 Note On,  0 -> ch1  no
```

lessons.title: Turn note numbers into frequencies
lessons.summary: MIDI specifies note numbers; the equal-tempered frequency calculation additionally assumes a tuning reference.
lessons.body:
Product details in this unit refer to the original Digitakt OS 1.53 manual and Digitakt II OS 1.17 manual, fetched on 16 October 2026. Confirm your model, firmware and current manual before wiring or configuring it.

## Note on and note off

The two messages your synth must handle first:

| Message | Status | Data 1 | Data 2 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Note Off | `0x8n` | key (0–127) | release velocity |
| Note On | `0x9n` | key (0–127) | velocity (0–127) |

The letter in the final hexadecimal position labels the channel nibble; it is not a literal hexadecimal digit. The key number identifies the note: the MIDI specification gives **middle C a value of 60**. Each step is a semitone, so 61 is C♯, 72 is the C an octave up.

Converting a key number to a frequency is a convention from the MIDI Tuning Standard and equal temperament: key 69 is A at 440 Hz, and each semitone multiplies the frequency by the same factor, the twelfth root of 2 (about 1.0595), so that twelve semitones exactly double it. Your oscillator needs this conversion every time a note starts:

```formula
f = 440 Hz × 2^{(n − 69) / 12}
f = 440 Hz × 2^{(60 − 69) / 12}
f = 440 Hz × 2^{−0.75}
f ≈ 261.63 Hz
where
f: the frequency the oscillator should play, in hertz (Hz)
n: the MIDI key number, 0 to 127; 60 is middle C, 69 is the A above it
440 Hz: the tuning anchor, the A above middle C (key 69)
Hz: hertz, cycles per second
2^{…}: 2 raised to the power in braces; a power of 1 doubles, −1 halves, 1/12 is one semitone up
≈: approximately equal to (the result is rounded)
In words: count semitones away from key 69, divide by 12 to get octaves, and double 440 Hz once per octave up (or halve it once per octave down).
```

Worked examples: key 81 is 12 semitones above 69, so the power is 1 and the frequency is 880 Hz; key 57 is 12 below, so the power is −1 and it is 220 Hz. This holds only for standard 12-tone equal temperament tuned to a 440 Hz reference A; a synth with a different tuning reference or a microtonal scale uses a different formula or table. The same calculation in Python:

```python
# Offline 12-TET tuning: note 69 is A440.
def note_to_hz(n):
    # A twelve-note change doubles
    # frequency.
    return 440.0 * 2 ** ((n - 69) / 12)

# Output is note number then hertz.
for n in (60, 69, 36):
    print(n, round(note_to_hz(n), 2))
```

```output
60 261.63
69 440.0
36 65.41
```

> [!note] Octave names differ, numbers don't
> Devices disagree about what to *call* note 60. Ableton Live's note ruler starts at C-2 (note 0), so Live calls middle C (60) **Live C3**. Elektron's Digitakt manuals number notes from Digitakt C0 (note 0, through Digitakt G10 for note 127); the original Digitakt manual states outright that MIDI note 60, middle C, is **Digitakt C5**. Much other software calls it C4. The number 60 is what goes on the wire, so debug with numbers.

## Key takeaways
- MIDI specifies note numbers; the equal-tempered frequency calculation additionally assumes a tuning reference.

options.explanation: Correct. 57 is 12 semitones below 69, which is exactly one octave down, halving the frequency.
This subtracts linearly (440 − 12.5). Pitch is exponential: each semitone multiplies frequency by the twelfth root of two.

options.text: 880 Hz

That is key 60 (middle C), three semitones above 57.

questions.workedExample:
Use the equal-temperament conversion from key number to frequency:

```formula
f = 440 Hz × 2^{(n − 69) / 12}
f = 440 Hz × 2^{(57 − 69) / 12}
f = 440 Hz × 2^{−1}
f = 220 Hz
where
f: the oscillator frequency, in hertz (Hz)
n: the MIDI key number; here 57
440 Hz: the tuning anchor, key 69 (the A above middle C)
Hz: hertz, cycles per second
2^{…}: 2 raised to the power in braces; a power of −1 means halve
In words: key 57 is 12 semitones (one octave) below key 69, so its frequency is half of 440 Hz.
```

Any 12-semitone step is an octave, a factor of 2. Your synth's pitch code should compute this (or read a 128-entry table) rather than scale linearly.

lessons.title: Handle velocity and both note endings
lessons.summary: Normalise Note On with velocity zero into a note-off event before voice handling.
lessons.body:
Velocity and note endings are separate from the key number. The synth must recognise both documented ways to release a MIDI note.

## Velocity


For a Note On that starts a note, velocity is a seven-bit performance value from 1 to 127, commonly representing how fast a key was struck. The specification leaves its interpretation to the receiver; it suggests that if velocity controls loudness, the mapping should preferably be exponential, and that devices without velocity sensing should send **64**.

### Note on with velocity 0 means note off

This rule trips up nearly every first MIDI implementation. The MIDI 1.0 specification gives two equivalent ways to end a note:

1. A Note Off message: `8n kk vv`.
2. A Note On message with velocity zero: `9n kk 00`.

It says a receiver **must be able to recognise either method, and should treat them identically**. Many transmitters prefer the second form because, combined with running status, a long run of notes can be sent without repeating the status byte.

If your synth treats `9n kk 00` as "start a note very quietly", notes will never end. That is a classic stuck-note bug.

## Key takeaways
- Normalise Note On with velocity zero into a note-off event before voice handling.

## Further reading

options.text: Start a second, silent instance of key 60

options.text: Ignore it, because Note On with velocity 0 is invalid
options.explanation: It is valid and widely used. The specification requires receivers to recognise it.

options.text: End key 60 on channel 1, exactly as if it had received `80 3C 40`
options.explanation: Correct. The spec says a receiver must be able to recognise both Note Off and Note On with velocity 0, and should treat them identically.

1. `90 3C 64`: Note On, channel 1, key 60, velocity 100. The note starts.
2. `90 3C 00`: same status and key, velocity 0.
3. The MIDI 1.0 spec (Note-Off section) defines two equivalent ways to end a note: Note Off (8n), or Note On with velocity zero. A receiver must recognise both and should treat them identically.
4. Good practice: normalise in the parser, converting `9n kk 00` to a note-off event, so the voice code only ever sees one kind of "off".

questions.prompt: Your synth plays correctly from a USB keyboard that sends `8n` note offs. Driven by a different sequencer, every note sustains forever. A MIDI monitor shows the sequencer sending `9n kk 00` to end notes. Which fix belongs in the parser?

options.explanation: The note offs would then be ignored, so the notes would still never end.

options.text: Ask the sequencer to send `8n` instead
options.explanation: Many transmitters legitimately use velocity-0 note ons (especially with running status). A receiver is required to accept both forms.

options.text: Convert `9n kk 00` into a note-off event before it reaches the voice code
options.explanation: Correct. That implements the spec rule that the two forms are identical, in one place, so voice allocation and envelopes see a single kind of note off.

options.text: Treat velocity 0 as velocity 1 so the note is at least audible
options.explanation: This turns the note off into a new note on, which makes the stuck-note problem worse.

questions.workedExample:
1. The two transmitters differ only in how they end notes.
2. MIDI 1.0 lets transmitters use either `8n kk vv` or `9n kk 00`; receivers must treat them identically.
3. The synth evidently handles only `8n`.
4. The robust fix is at the boundary: as soon as the parser completes a `9n` message with velocity 0, emit a note-off event. Everything downstream stays simple.

lessons.title: Build and decode complete messages
lessons.summary: Trace status, channel, key and velocity separately, and check MIDI and audio paths independently.
lessons.body:
Product details in this unit refer to the original Digitakt OS 1.53 manual and Digitakt II OS 1.17 manual, fetched on 16 October 2026. Confirm your model, firmware and current manual before wiring or configuring it.

## Building and reading messages

Here is the byte-level construction in Python. Your firmware will do the same with integers and bit operations.

```python
def note_on(channel, note, velocity):
    # Inputs are prevalidated MIDI values.
    # Convert displayed channel to
    # wire form.
    status = 0x90 | (channel - 1)
    return bytes([status, note, velocity])

def note_off(channel, note, velocity=64):
    # Use the explicit Note Off status.
    status = 0x80 | (channel - 1)
    return bytes([status, note, velocity])

# Output is hexadecimal bytes in wire order.
print(note_on(1, 60, 100).hex(" "))
print(note_on(10, 36, 127).hex(" "))
print(note_off(16, 69).hex(" "))
```

```output
90 3c 64
99 24 7f
8f 45 40
```

Read the first line: `0x90` is Note On, channel nibble 0 (channel 1); `0x3C` is 60, middle C; `0x64` is velocity 100.

Decoding goes the other way. Shift the status byte right by four bits to get the message type, and mask off its top nibble to get the wire channel:

```formula
M = S >> 4
ch = (S & 0x0F) + 1
M = 0x93 >> 4 = 0x9
ch = (0x93 & 0x0F) + 1 = 3 + 1 = 4
where
M: the message type, the status byte's top nibble, in hexadecimal: 8 = Note Off, 9 = Note On, B = Control Change
S: the received status byte, here 0x93
ch: the channel as people number it, 1 to 16
>>: bitwise right shift, moving every bit down by the given number of places and discarding the bits that fall off; shifting by 4 keeps just the top nibble
&: bitwise AND, which keeps only the bits that are set in both values; AND with 0x0F (binary 0000 1111) keeps just the low nibble
0x: prefix meaning hexadecimal (base 16)
In words: the top four bits say what kind of message it is, and the bottom four bits plus one say which channel.
```

Then fold velocity-0 note ons into note offs at the earliest point, so the rest of the synth only ever sees one kind of "off":

```python
# Fragment assumes one valid note message.
def describe(msg):
    status, note, vel = msg
    kind = status >> 4      # top nibble
    ch = (status & 0x0F) + 1
    # Both legal endings become one action.
    is_off = kind == 0x8 or (
        kind == 0x9 and vel == 0)
    if is_off:
        return f"ch{ch} off {note}"
    if kind == 0x9:
        return f"ch{ch} on {note} vel {vel}"
    return "other"

print(describe(bytes([0x93, 0x40, 0x50])))
print(describe(bytes([0x93, 0x40, 0x00])))
print(describe(bytes([0x83, 0x40, 0x40])))
```

```output
ch4 on 64 vel 80
ch4 off 64
ch4 off 64
```

## A worked example

A sequencer plays a two-note phrase on channel 3: key 64 (E above middle C) at velocity 90, released, then key 67 (G) at velocity 110, released. On the wire, using explicit note offs with the recommended release velocity of 64:

```
92 40 5A   note on  ch3 key 64 vel 90
82 40 40   note off ch3 key 64
92 43 6E   note on  ch3 key 67 vel 110
82 43 40   note off ch3 key 67
```

Twelve bytes, about 3.84 ms of wire time in total. The receiver needs to know only the channel it is listening on to decide whether to act on them.

## Pitfalls to design out early

- **Ignoring velocity-0 note on.** Stuck notes. Normalise it in the parser.
- **Channel off-by-one.** Your synth "doesn't respond" because it listens on 0x01 while the Digitakt sends on 0x00.
- **Assuming 8-bit values.** Data bytes never exceed 127. A value of 128 or more is a status byte; MIDI real-time statuses can interleave without replacing the current message.
- **Treating MIDI as sound.** If you hear nothing, check the audio path separately from the MIDI path. A MIDI monitor on the computer can prove the MIDI half works.
- **Unmatched note offs.** The specification requires a transmitter to send a note off for every note on. Your receiver still has to cope with missing ones; the later stuck-note unit covers recovery.

## Key takeaways
- Trace status, channel, key and velocity separately, and check MIDI and audio paths independently.

## Further reading

options.explanation: Correct. 0x8 = Note Off, nibble 0xF = channel 16, 0x45 = 69, 0x40 = 64 (the spec's recommended release velocity when none is measured).

The channel conversion in the second line:

```formula

```

Key 69 is the A at 440 Hz (key 60 is middle C, and 69 is nine semitones higher). A release velocity of 64 is what the specification recommends a device sends when it doesn't measure release velocity.

lessons.title: Read message lengths and pressure
lessons.summary: Program Change and Channel Pressure have one data byte; distinguish one pressure value per channel from one per key.
lessons.body:
Product details in this unit refer to the original Digitakt OS 1.53 manual and Digitakt II OS 1.17 manual, fetched on 16 October 2026. Confirm your model, firmware and current manual before wiring or configuring it.

Note on and note off make a synth play. Everything else in MIDI makes it *expressive* and *in time*: knobs and wheels (control change), patch selection (program change), pitch bend, pressure, the tempo clock, and manufacturer-specific data (SysEx).

This unit maps message lengths and pressure. The following units cover controllers, running status, system messages and MIDI 2.0.

## The full map

Channel messages carry a channel in the low nibble of the status byte (the final placeholder stands for a wire channel from zero to fifteen). System messages (`0xF0`–`0xFF`) have no channel.

| Status | Message | Data bytes |
|---|---|---|
| `8n` | Note Off | key, velocity |
| `9n` | Note On | key, velocity |
| `An` | Poly Key Pressure | key, pressure |
| `Bn` | Control Change | controller, value |
| `Cn` | Program Change | program |
| `Dn` | Channel Pressure | pressure |
| `En` | Pitch Bend | MIDI LSB, MIDI MSB |
| `F0`…`F7` | System Exclusive / Common | varies |
| `F8`…`FF` | System Real-Time | none |

Notice that Program Change and Channel Pressure have **one** data byte; the other channel messages have two. A parser must know this table to tell where one message ends and the next begins.

## Aftertouch (pressure)

Pressing harder on a key after it bottoms out can send:

- **Channel Pressure** `Dn vv`: one value for the whole channel (the MIDI Association's message summary says to send the single greatest pressure of the keys held).
- **Poly Key Pressure** `An kk vv`: a separate value per key.

The receiver decides what pressure does: volume, brightness, vibrato. The Digitakt's MIDI tracks have an "AT" parameter that sends aftertouch to the external synth.

## Key takeaways
- Program Change and Channel Pressure have one data byte; distinguish one pressure value per channel from one per key.

## Further reading

lessons.summary: Check the published CC allocation and document the numbers your synth accepts.
lessons.body:
Product details in this unit refer to the original Digitakt OS 1.53 manual and Digitakt II OS 1.17 manual, fetched on 16 October 2026. Confirm your model, firmware and current manual before wiring or configuring it.

## Control change

`Bn cc vv`: controller number `cc` (0–119) set to value `vv` (0–127). Controllers 120–127 use the same status byte but are **Channel Mode messages** (covered in **Handle SysEx and channel mode messages**).

Commonly met controllers, from the MIDI Association's control change table:

| CC | Defined as |
|---|---|
| 0 / 32 | Bank Select MIDI MSB / MIDI LSB |
| 1 | Modulation wheel |
| 7 | Channel Volume |
| 10 | Pan |
| 11 | Expression |
| 64 | Sustain pedal (≤63 off, ≥64 on) |
| 71 | Sound Ctrl 2 (default: timbre) |
| 72 / 73 | Sound Ctrl 3 / 4 (release / attack) |
| 74 | Sound Ctrl 5 (default: brightness) |

Many synths map CC 74 to filter cutoff and CC 71 to resonance, following those "brightness" and "timbre" defaults, but nothing forces this. Plenty of CC numbers (for example 20–31 and 102–119) are listed as **undefined**, which makes them a sensible home for your synth's own parameters. Whatever you choose, document it in a table: the specification asks manufacturers to publish a controller allocation table, and you will need it yourself when setting up the Digitakt.

## Key takeaways
- Check the published CC allocation and document the numbers your synth accepts.

lessons.title: Combine coarse and fine controllers
lessons.summary: Pair the first 32 controller numbers with their fine controllers, and reset the remembered fine value on a new coarse value.
lessons.body:
## 14-bit controllers


128 steps are coarse for something like filter cutoff: you can hear each step as a zipper. The specification pairs controllers so that **CC 0–31 carry MIDI coarse parts and CC 32–63 carry the matching MIDI fine parts**. The MIDI LSB's controller number is always 32 more than the MIDI MSB's:

```formula
c_LSB = c_MSB + 32
c_LSB = 1 + 32 = 33
where
c_MSB: the controller number that carries the coarse (most significant) 7 bits, 0 to 31; here CC 1, the modulation wheel
c_LSB: the controller number that carries the fine (least significant) 7 bits, 32 to 63
In words: the fine half of any of the first 32 controllers lives 32 numbers higher, so CC 1 pairs with CC 33 and CC 7 with CC 39.
```

Together the two 7-bit halves give 14 bits, and the combined value is the MIDI MSB scaled up by 128 plus the MIDI LSB:

```formula
v = 128 MSB + LSB
v = 64 × 128 + 32
v = 8224
v_max = 127 × 128 + 127 = 16383
where
v: the combined 14-bit controller value, 0 to 16,383 (16,384 steps)
MSB: the coarse seven-bit part, a dimensionless integer from zero to 127
LSB: the fine seven-bit part, 0 to 127 (the fine part)
v_max: the largest possible combined value
In words: the coarse byte counts in steps of 128 and the fine byte fills in between, giving 128 × 128 = 16,384 steps instead of 128.
```

Multiplying by 128 is the same as applying a bitwise left shift by 7 bits, which is how firmware usually writes it: `(msb << 7) | lsb`.

Rules worth implementing exactly:

- If 128 steps are enough, a transmitter can send only the MIDI MSB.
- After both have been sent, a fine change may send just the MIDI LSB.
- **When a MIDI MSB arrives, the receiver should reset its MIDI LSB to zero.**

So `B0 01 40` then `B0 21 20` means modulation is 8,224: MIDI MSB 0x40 (64) and MIDI LSB 0x20 (32), exactly the worked example above.

## Key takeaways
- Pair the first 32 controller numbers with their fine controllers, and reset the remembered fine value on a new coarse value.

## Further reading

This keeps the old MIDI LSB of 32 (65 × 128 + 32). The spec says a new MIDI MSB resets the MIDI LSB to zero.
That was the value after the second message (64 × 128 + 32), before the MIDI MSB changed.
The receiver should scale the MIDI MSB into the top 7 bits of the 14-bit value, not treat it as the whole value.


1. `B0 01 40`: MIDI MSB 64, MIDI LSB reset to 0, giving 64 × 128 + 0 = 8,192.
2. `B0 21 20`: CC 33 is the MIDI LSB of CC 1, so MIDI LSB becomes 32, giving 64 × 128 + 32 = 8,224.
3. `B0 01 41`: a new MIDI MSB of 65. The specification requires the receiver to reset its MIDI LSB value to zero when this new MIDI MSB arrives. So the value is 65 × 128 + 0 = 8,320.

If the sender wants a fine value it follows up with another MIDI LSB.

lessons.title: Select parameters, banks and programs
lessons.summary: Use RPN selection before Data Entry, deselect when done, and apply a selected bank when Program Change arrives.
lessons.body:
## RPN: setting pitch-bend range


Registered Parameter Numbers (RPNs) select a parameter with CC 101 (MIDI MSB) and CC 100 (MIDI LSB), then set it with Data Entry (CC 6, plus CC 38 for fine). RPN 0,0 is **pitch bend sensitivity**: Data Entry MIDI MSB is semitones, MIDI LSB is cents. To set ±12 semitones on channel 1, a sender transmits:

```
B0 65 00   RPN MSB = 0
B0 64 00   RPN LSB = 0 (bend range)
B0 06 0C   data entry: 12 semitones
B0 26 00   data entry LSB: 0 cents
```

Sending RPN 127,127 (the "null" RPN) afterwards stops later Data Entry messages changing it by accident. NRPNs (CC 99/98) work the same way for manufacturer-defined parameters; the Elektron manuals list which NRPNs their knobs send.

## Program change and bank select

`Cn pp` selects patch `pp`, with a single data byte. Programs are 0–127 on the wire, but many devices display them as 1–128, so the off-by-one appears again.

For more than 128 patches, the specification has the sender transmit Bank Select as a pair (CC 0 MIDI MSB, CC 32 MIDI LSB), immediately followed by the Program Change. Bank Select alone must not change the program; the new bank applies when the Program Change arrives.

## Key takeaways
- Use RPN selection before Data Entry, deselect when done, and apply a selected bank when Program Change arrives.

lessons.title: Pack and unpack pitch bend
lessons.summary: Pitch bend sends its low seven bits first and centres at 8,192 rather than zero.
lessons.body:
## Pitch bend

`En ll mm` carries a 14-bit value, **least significant 7 bits first**. Unlike other controllers, the specification says pitch bend is always sent with both data bytes, because the ear is very sensitive to pitch.

- Minimum: `00 00` = 0.
- **Centre (no bend): `00 40` = 0x2000 = 8,192.**
- Maximum: `7F 7F` = 16,383.

To send a bend value you split it into two 7-bit halves; to receive one you join them again. The splitting uses a mask and a shift:

```formula
LSB = v & 0x7F
MSB = (v >> 7) & 0x7F
v = (MSB << 7) | LSB
LSB = 8192 & 0x7F = 0x00
MSB = (8192 >> 7) & 0x7F = 0x40
where
v: the 14-bit bend value, 0 to 16,383; centre 8,192
LSB: the first data byte sent, holding the low 7 bits
MSB: the second data byte sent, holding the high 7 bits
&: bitwise AND, keeping only bits set in both values; AND with 0x7F (binary 0111 1111) keeps the low 7 bits
>>: bitwise right shift by the given number of bits (dividing by 128 for a shift of 7, discarding the remainder)
<<: bitwise left shift by the given number of bits (multiplying by 128 for a shift of 7)
|: bitwise OR, combining the bits of both values
0x: prefix meaning hexadecimal (base 16); 0x7F is 127 and 0x40 is 64
In words: the low seven bits go in the first byte and the next seven bits in the second; joining them back gives the original value.
```

The same in Python:

```python
def bend_bytes(value):
    # value 0..16383, centre 8192
    # Mask the fine seven bits for byte one.
    lsb = value & 0x7F
    # Shift the coarse part into low bits.
    msb = (value >> 7) & 0x7F
    return lsb, msb

def bend_value(lsb, msb):
    return (msb << 7) | lsb

# Output: raw value, fine byte, coarse byte.
for v in (0, 8192, 16383, 12288):
    lsb, msb = bend_bytes(v)
    print(v, hex(lsb), hex(msb))

print(bend_value(0x00, 0x40))
```

```output
0 0x0 0x0
8192 0x0 0x40
16383 0x7f 0x7f
12288 0x0 0x60
8192
```

## Key takeaways
- Pitch bend sends its low seven bits first and centres at 8,192 rather than zero.

## Further reading
- [MIDI 1.0 Control Change Messages — MIDI Association](https://midi.org/midi-1-0-control-change-messages)

That is the maximum value, full upward bend.
Correct. Fine part zero and coarse part 64 encode the centre value of 8,192, hexadecimal 0x2000.
The byte order is MIDI LSB first, then MIDI MSB. This is MIDI LSB 64, MIDI MSB 0 = 64, almost full downward bend.

2. It is sent MIDI LSB first: `En ll mm`.
3. Split 8,192:

```formula

MSB = (v >> 7) & 0x7F
LSB = 8192 & 0x7F = 0x00
MSB = (8192 >> 7) & 0x7F
MSB = 64 & 0x7F = 0x40
where
v: the 14-bit bend value, 0 to 16,383

In words: 8,192 is exactly 64 × 128, so its low 7 bits are all zero and its high 7 bits are 64 (0x40).
```

lessons.title: Map pitch bend into a pitch offset
lessons.summary: Make the bend mapping explicit, keep centre exact, and account for the one-step asymmetry of the raw value range.
lessons.body:
## Choosing the pitch-bend range
How far is "full bend"? The receiver decides, or it is set via RPN 0. A ±2 semitone range is a common default. To turn the raw value into a pitch offset, measure how far it is from centre as a fraction of half the range, then scale by the bend range:

```formula
s = ((v − 8192) / 8192)r
s = ((12288 − 8192) / 8192) × 2
s = (4096 / 8192) × 2 = 1
where
s: the pitch offset in semitones; negative bends down, positive bends up
v: the received 14-bit bend value, 0 to 16,383
8192: the centre value, meaning no bend
r: the bend range in semitones, set by the receiver or by RPN 0; 2 here (±2 semitones)
In words: a value 4,096 counts above centre bends up by half the configured range with this mapping, here one semitone.
```

To apply the offset, scale the note's frequency by the same semitone factor as the key-to-frequency formula in the note-frequency unit:

```formula
f_bent = f 2^{s / 12}
f_bent = 440 Hz × 2^{1 / 12}
f_bent ≈ 466.16 Hz
where
f_bent: the frequency actually played with the bend applied, in hertz (Hz)
f: the frequency of the held note without bend, in hertz; here 440 Hz (key 69)
s: the bend offset in semitones from the formula above; here +1
Hz: hertz, cycles per second
2^{…}: 2 raised to the power in braces; a power of 1/12 is one semitone up
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: bending A 440 up one semitone gives the B♭ just above it, about 466 Hz.
```

Mapping the raw value to semitones in Python:

```python
def bend_semitones(value, rng=2):
    # rng = bend range in semitones (RPN 0)
    # Keep 8192 exactly at the zero offset.
    return (value - 8192) / 8192 * rng

# Output: raw value then semitone offset.
for v in (0, 8192, 12288, 16383):
    print(v, round(bend_semitones(v), 4))
```

```output
0 -2.0
8192 0.0
12288 1.0
16383 1.9998
```

The range is asymmetric by one step (8,192 values below centre, 8,191 above). This is an implementation mapping, not a MIDI-mandated bend law. An implementation can instead divide the upper half by 8,191 to make the maximum reach exactly the configured positive range; keep the centre exactly zero and document the choice.

> [!warning] Reset bend to centre, not zero
> A raw value of 0 is *full downward* bend. Initialise and reset pitch bend to 8,192. The spec's "Reset All Controllers" (CC 121) likewise returns pitch bend to centre.

## Key takeaways
- Make the bend mapping explicit, keep centre exact, and account for the one-step asymmetry of the raw value range.


lessons.title: Preserve and clear running status
lessons.summary: Reuse only channel status; System Common and SysEx clear it, while MIDI real-time bytes leave it and partial messages intact.
lessons.body:
## Running status

Running status is a byte-saving rule for **channel voice and mode messages**: once a status byte has been sent, the transmitter can omit it for following messages of the same type and channel, and send only the data bytes.

```
full:     90 3C 64  90 40 64  90 43 64
running:  90 3C 64     40 64     43 64
```

Nine bytes become seven. Combined with "note on, velocity 0 = note off", a whole melody can go out with a single `90` at the start.

The receiver's rules, from the specification and its appendix:

1. Remember the last channel status byte in a **running status buffer**.
2. A data byte that arrives when a complete message has just ended reuses that status.
3. Any new channel status byte replaces it.
4. **System Exclusive and System Common** status bytes clear it.
5. **Real-time bytes do not touch it**, even when they arrive between data bytes.

Running status is optional for transmitters but mandatory for receivers. The parser state-machine unit turns these rules into executable code.

## Key takeaways
- Reuse only channel status; System Common and SysEx clear it, while MIDI real-time bytes leave it and partial messages intact.

## Further reading
- [MIDI 1.0 Control Change Messages — MIDI Association](https://midi.org/midi-1-0-control-change-messages)

options.explanation: Under running status, data bytes after a complete channel message reuse the last status. They are not orphans.

options.text: Note on 60, note on 64, note on 67 at velocity 0, which it plays very quietly
options.explanation: Velocity 0 in a Note On means Note Off. Playing it quietly would leave a stuck note.

options.text: Note on 60, note on 64, and note on 67 at velocity 0, which it treats as note off 67
options.explanation: Correct. All three messages reuse status `90`; the last has velocity 0, so it is a note off.

Group the bytes, carrying the status forward:

```

   40 64 -> on  key 64 vel 100

```

questions.prompt: The receiver sees `90 3C F8 64`. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: The `F8` is a Timing Clock and should be acted on (or ignored) immediately
options.explanation: Correct. Real-time messages can appear anywhere, even between the data bytes of another message.

options.text: The `F8` aborts the Note On, so `64` is an orphan data byte
options.explanation: Only a new channel, System Common or SysEx status cancels an incomplete message. The interleaved timing byte leaves it intact.

options.text: After the `F8`, the parser resumes the Note On and completes it with velocity `64` (100)
options.explanation: Correct. The receiver returns to the previous status and completes `90 3C 64`.

options.text: The running status buffer is unchanged by the `F8`
options.explanation: Correct. The spec says MIDI real-time messages should not affect running status.

options.text: The receiver should now treat `F8` as the running status
options.explanation: Real-time messages are never stored as running status.

questions.workedExample:
1. `90 3C`: Note On started; one data byte still needed.
2. `F8`: a real-time byte. Handle it on its own (tick the clock, or ignore it if clock isn't used). Do **not** touch the partial message or the running status.
3. `64`: the missing velocity. Emit Note On key 60 velocity 100.

The spec allows MIDI real-time bytes "between Status and Data bytes of any other MIDI messages" precisely so clock timing isn't delayed by long messages.

questions.prompt: A receiver gets `B0 4A 50 F0 7D 01 F7 4A 60`. What happens to the final `4A 60`?

options.text: It is applied as CC 74 = 96 using running status from `B0`
options.explanation: The intervening SysEx cleared the running status buffer, so there is no status to reuse.

options.text: It is treated as more SysEx data
options.explanation: `F7` ended the SysEx. Bytes after it are not part of the exclusive message.

options.text: It is ignored, because SysEx cleared the running status
options.explanation: Correct. The spec's appendix: the running status buffer is cleared when a System Exclusive or System Common status is received, and data bytes are ignored while the buffer is empty.

options.text: It is applied as Note On key 74 velocity 96
options.explanation: There is no Note On status anywhere in the stream.

```
B0 4A 50 -> CC 74 = 80, ch1
           (buffer = B0)
F0       -> SysEx start
           (buffer cleared)
7D 01    -> SysEx data
F7       -> End of Exclusive
4A 60    -> no status: ignore
```

A transmitter that wants this second CC to be received must resend `B0`. Good transmitters refresh the status byte after SysEx or System Common; System Real-Time preserves running status.

lessons.title: Interpret clock, transport and sensing
lessons.summary: MIDI clock has 24 ticks per quarter note; transport and optional Active Sensing have distinct jobs.
lessons.body:
Product details in this unit refer to the original Digitakt OS 1.53 manual and Digitakt II OS 1.17 manual, fetched on 16 October 2026. Confirm your model, firmware and current manual before wiring or configuring it.

## System real-time: clock and transport

Real-time messages are single status bytes with no data. They may appear **anywhere**, even in the middle of another message, so they can keep accurate time.

| Byte | Message |
|---|---|
| `F8` | Timing Clock |
| `FA` | Start |
| `0xFB` | Continue |
| `0xFC` | Stop |
| `FE` | Active Sensing |
| `FF` | System Reset |

`F9` and `FD` are undefined and should be ignored.

**Timing Clock is sent 24 times per quarter note** (24 PPQN, pulses per quarter note). A receiver measures the gap between clocks to find the tempo. Going the other way, the expected gap at a given tempo is one minute divided by the number of clocks in that minute:

```formula
t_clk = 60 s / (BPM × PPQN)
t_clk = 60 s / (120 × 24)
t_clk = 60 s / 2880
t_clk ≈ 0.020833 s ≈ 20.833 ms
where
t_clk: the time between consecutive Timing Clock (F8) bytes, in seconds (s) or milliseconds (ms)
BPM: tempo in beats (quarter notes) per minute; 120 here
PPQN: pulses per quarter note, fixed at 24 for MIDI clock
60 s: the number of seconds in a minute
s: seconds
ms: milliseconds, thousandths of a second
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: at 120 BPM there are 2,880 clocks a minute, so one arrives roughly every 20.8 ms.
```

Faster tempos give shorter gaps: at 60 BPM the gap is about 41.7 ms. A receiver can turn the formula round (the tempo in BPM is 60 seconds divided by 24 times the measured gap) to estimate tempo; in practice it averages several gaps, because individual clocks jitter. The same calculation in Python:

```python
def clock_interval_ms(bpm, ppqn=24):
    # Treat one beat as a quarter note here.
    beats_per_s = bpm / 60
    # Convert seconds per tick to
    # milliseconds.
    return 1000 / (beats_per_s * ppqn)

for bpm in (60, 120, 140):
    ms = clock_interval_ms(bpm)
    print(bpm, round(ms, 3))
```

```output
60 41.667
120 20.833
140 17.857
```

Six clocks make one sixteenth note, which is the unit the **Song Position Pointer** (`F2 ll mm`) counts in. Transport details from the specification:

- **Start** (`FA`) means play from the beginning. **Continue** (`0xFB`) means resume from the current position. A synced receiver starts on the *next* `F8` after either, and the specification asks senders to leave at least 1 ms between `FA` and the first `F8`.
- **Stop** (`0xFC`) should stop playback immediately.
- Clocks may keep flowing while stopped, so receivers can lock to tempo before Start.

**Active Sensing** (`FE`) is optional. Once a receiver has seen it, it should expect some message at least every 300 ms. If all MIDI traffic stops for the timeout, it should silence its voices and leave Active Sensing mode; silence can indicate disconnection, but does not prove the physical cause. The detailed specification recommends sending within 270 ms and judging loss after more than 330 ms to leave timing margin around the nominal 300 ms interval.

A simple mono synth needs clock only for tempo-synced features such as an arpeggiator or a synced LFO. It must still *tolerate* clock bytes, because a sequencer like the Digitakt may send them constantly.

## Key takeaways
- MIDI clock has 24 ticks per quarter note; transport and optional Active Sensing have distinct jobs.

## Further reading

- [MIDI 1.0 Detailed Specification 4.2.1 (archived copy at CCRMA)](https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~esteban/teaching/McGill_MUMT306/M1_v4-2-1_MIDI_1-0_Detailed_Specification_96-1-4.pdf)
- [Details about MIDI 2.0, MIDI-CI, Profiles and Property Exchange — MIDI Association](https://midi.org/details-about-midi-2-0-midi-ci-profiles-and-property-exchange-updated-june-2023)
- [MIDI 2.0 — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MIDI_2.0)

options.explanation: 24 is the number per quarter note, and a 4/4 bar has four quarter notes.
Correct. 24 clocks per quarter note × 4 quarter notes = 96 clocks per bar.
That is the number of sixteenth notes in the bar. Each sixteenth is six clocks.
That would be one clock per beat. MIDI clock is much finer than that.

options.text: 20 ms

```formula
t_clk = 60 s / (BPM × PPQN)

where
t_clk: the time between consecutive F8 bytes, in seconds (s) or milliseconds (ms)

60 s: one minute in seconds

ms: milliseconds, thousandths of a second
In words: at 125 BPM there are 3,000 clocks a minute, which is 50 a second, so one every 20 ms.
```

So 20 ms between clocks. A synced arpeggiator can estimate tempo by averaging several intervals, since individual clocks jitter by up to one DIN framed-byte duration or more.

lessons.title: Handle SysEx and channel mode messages
lessons.summary: Keep SysEx data seven-bit and respect ID allocation; distinguish channel-wide mode messages from ordinary sound controls.
lessons.body:
Product details in this unit refer to the original Digitakt OS 1.53 manual and Digitakt II OS 1.17 manual, fetched on 16 October 2026. Confirm your model, firmware and current manual before wiring or configuring it.

## System Exclusive

SysEx carries manufacturer-defined data: patch dumps, firmware, parameter edits.

```
F0 <id> <data ...> F7
```

- The ID is 1 byte, or 3 bytes starting with `00`.
- Every SysEx payload byte is a data byte (0–127); independent MIDI real-time status bytes may interleave on the wire. 8-bit data must be packed into 7-bit bytes.
- **ID `7D` is reserved for non-commercial use** (education, research): suitable for a private experiment, not for a product released to the public even free of charge.
- IDs `7E` and `7F` are the **Universal SysEx** messages (7E for Universal Non-Real-Time and 7F for Universal Real-Time) defined by the MIDI specs themselves.
- Only MIDI real-time bytes may be interleaved inside a SysEx message. Any other status byte terminates it, although senders should always end with `F7`.

The Digitakt uses SysEx to send and receive project, pattern and Sound data (presets on the Digitakt II) through its SYSEX DUMP menu, which is a handy backup route.

## Channel mode messages

CC numbers 120–127 are mode messages:

| CC | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 120 | All Sound Off (silence now) |
| 121 | Reset All Controllers |
| 122 | Local Control on/off |
| 123 | All Notes Off |
| 124–127 | MIDI omni mode, MIDI monophonic mode and MIDI polyphonic mode |

Channel Mode messages are recognised on the receiver’s configured Basic Channel, even when Omni is on. MIDI monophonic mode concerns note voices: with Omni off it can allocate one voice per selected MIDI channel; with Omni on it plays one voice across the received channels. MIDI polyphonic mode permits simultaneous voices up to the receiver’s capacity. Neither mode specifies mono or stereo audio output.

All Notes Off and the mode changes also perform the specified note-release functions when supported. In particular, the specification says to ignore CC 123 while Omni is on. All Sound Off silences sound promptly, without waiting for the normal release envelope. Sustain deferral and recovery are developed in the stuck-note unit.

## Key takeaways
- Keep SysEx data seven-bit and respect ID allocation; distinguish channel-wide mode messages from ordinary sound controls.

lessons.body:
Product details in this unit refer to the original Digitakt OS 1.53 manual and Digitakt II OS 1.17 manual, fetched on 16 October 2026. Confirm your model, firmware and current manual before wiring or configuring it.

## MIDI 2.0 in one section

MIDI 2.0 (announced in January 2020, core specifications updated in June 2023) **extends** MIDI 1.0 rather than replacing it. The headline changes, from the MIDI Association:

- The **Universal MIDI Packet (UMP)** replaces the byte stream with 32-, 64-, 96- or 128-bit packets. UMP can carry both MIDI 1.0 and MIDI 2.0 messages, organised as 16 groups of 16 channels.
- **Higher resolution**: velocity is 16-bit; control changes, pressure and pitch bend are 32-bit.
- **Per-note** controllers and pitch, and thousands of additional registered and assignable controllers.
- **MIDI-CI** (Capability Inquiry) lets two devices discover each other's features. Profiles and Property Exchange (JSON-based) build on it.
- Optional **Jitter Reduction timestamps**.
- **USB MIDI 2.0** carries UMP natively and can fall back to USB MIDI 1.0.

For the documented DIN connection in this example, MIDI 1.0 is a practical initial target; this does not select the project's final hardware or architecture. The Digitakt manuals describe MIDI 1.0 facilities (notes, CC, NRPN, program change, clock), and DIN MIDI carries the MIDI 1.0 byte stream. MIDI 2.0 becomes interesting if you later want very high-resolution or per-note control from a computer over USB.

## Key takeaways
- UMP and higher-resolution messages extend the ecosystem; choose supported transports and features for the actual devices.

lessons.title: Separate receiving from audio work
lessons.summary: Receive into bounded storage, count overflow, and keep parsing, waiting and logging outside the audio deadline.
lessons.body:
The preceding MIDI units established the message formats. The implementation units cover what firmware has to do with them: turn a stream of bytes into events, decide which note a monophonic synth should play, make sure notes always stop, and turn controller values into smooth parameter changes.

The code here is Python, so you can run and test the logic on your computer first. On the synth, the same logic runs in firmware. Where timing and threads matter, the lesson uses short language-neutral pseudocode.

## Where MIDI handling runs

A typical embedded synth has three activities:

```diagram
UART RX interrupt  ->  byte FIFO
                          |
main loop / control task: parse,
  note priority, CC mapping
                          |
           event queue + parameters
                          |
audio callback: oscillators,
  envelopes, smoothing
```

- **Receiving** happens in an interrupt (or via DMA). It should only push each byte into a fixed-size ring buffer. At 31,250 baud successive bytes can complete every 320 µs at the nominal bit rate.
- **Parsing and note logic** run outside the audio callback, in the main loop or a control task, draining the buffer.
- **The audio callback** consumes a bounded number of queued note events in order, applies them to its voice state, and smooths latest-value control parameters. It must never wait on MIDI, allocate memory, or print logs.

How data crosses from the control code to the audio callback (atomics, a lock-free queue, or double buffering) depends on your platform, and is covered with embedded programming. The rule for now: the audio callback must never block.

```text
on_uart_byte(b):            # interrupt
    if not fifo.push(b):
        overflow_count += 1  # never block

control_loop():
    while fifo.pop(b):
        for event in parser.feed(b):
            handle(event)
```

This is architectural pseudocode, not executable Python: buffer, parser and event interfaces must be supplied by the platform. An interrupt may receive batches through a hardware FIFO or DMA rather than one callback per byte.

Count overflows rather than ignoring them. A lost note-off byte is a future stuck note, and the counter tells you it happened.

## Key takeaways
- Receive into bounded storage, count overflow, and keep parsing, waiting and logging outside the audio deadline.

## Further reading

questions.prompt: Which part must deliver each audio block by a fixed deadline and must therefore never wait for MIDI input?

options.text: The UART receive interrupt
options.explanation: The interrupt runs because a byte has arrived; it pushes it into a buffer and returns. It doesn't wait either, but it isn't the component the question is about.

options.text: The parser in the main loop
options.explanation: The main loop polls the ring buffer and processes whatever is there, but it isn't the one with the hard audio deadline.

options.text: None: all parts may block briefly because MIDI is slow
options.explanation: No. Waiting for input has no finite guaranteed completion time, however slow MIDI is.

options.text: The audio callback
options.explanation: Correct. Consume ordered note events from fixed-size ordered event storage and read latest control targets without waiting; a latest-note mailbox can lose transitions.

questions.workedExample:
DIN bytes can be 320 µs apart, and an incomplete message can stall indefinitely. The audio callback has a hard deadline: it must finish each block before the converter needs the next one.

```formula
t_block = N / f_s
t_block = 48 / (48000 Hz)
t_block = 0.001 s = 1 ms
where
t_block: the duration of one block, in seconds (s); processing must finish with margin inside the actual platform deadline
N: the number of samples per audio block; 48 in this example
f_s: the sample rate, in samples per second (hertz, Hz); 48,000 here
Hz: hertz, here samples per second
s: seconds
ms: milliseconds, thousandths of a second
In words: a 48-sample block at 48 kHz lasts 1 ms, so the available processing budget is at most that duration and also has to leave room for interrupt and scheduling overhead, whatever MIDI is doing.
```

So it consumes only available queued events with a bounded budget and reads latest control targets. Neither the UART ISR nor callback should block; parsing belongs outside the callback.

questions.prompt: At the nominal DIN rate, successive byte completions are 320 µs apart. An initially empty UART byte buffer may go 10 ms without a drain. How many usable byte slots cover that gap, and what is a sensible allocation?

options.text: 4 bytes, because MIDI messages are at most 3 bytes
options.explanation: Between two runs of the control loop many messages can arrive, not just one.

options.text: 31,250 bytes, one second of data
options.explanation: Far more than needed. The buffer only has to cover the longest gap between drains.

options.text: No buffer is needed if the UART has a hardware FIFO
options.explanation: Typical UART hardware FIFOs hold only a few bytes, much less than 10 ms of data.

options.text: 32 usable slots cover the stated gap; choose 64 or more and check the ring’s reserved slot
options.explanation: Correct. Depending on arrival phase, up to 32 byte completions fit in that gap. Add margin for longer service gaps. A ring that reserves one storage slot needs an allocation larger than its usable capacity.

questions.workedExample:
```formula
r_max = R / N_bits
r_max = (31250 bit/s) / (10 bit)
r_max = 3125 B/s
n = t_gap r_max
n = 0.010 s × 3125 B/s
n = 31.25 B
where
r_max: the most bytes per second DIN MIDI can deliver, in bytes per second (B/s)
R: the DIN MIDI bit rate, 31,250 bits per second (bit/s)
N_bits: bits per framed byte: 1 start + 8 data + 1 stop = 10
bit: one binary digit
B: byte
t_gap: the longest time between two runs of the control loop, 10 ms = 0.010 s
s: seconds
n: the continuous-rate occupancy estimate in bytes, not an integer upper bound on arrival completions
In words: DIN MIDI delivers at most 3,125 bytes a second (one every 0.32 ms), so in a 10 ms gap up to 32 complete bytes may accumulate depending on the starting alignment.
```

So provide at least 32 usable byte slots. A circular buffer implementation may reserve one extra slot to distinguish full from empty. Add margin for occasional longer gaps (and delayed servicing; DIN SysEx does not exceed the same line rate), and pick a power of two: 64 or 128 bytes costs almost nothing. Keep counting overflows to confirm it is enough.
