lessons.title: Trace a MIDI parser state machine
lessons.summary: Test single-data-byte messages, interrupted messages, SysEx termination and orphan data on the computer.
lessons.body:
## Parsing: a small state machine

The parser must cope with everything the specification allows:

- channel messages with one or two data bytes;
- **running status** (data bytes with no new status byte);
- **MIDI real-time messages** (single bytes `F8`–`FF`) arriving anywhere, even mid-message;
- SysEx of any length without accumulating its payload;
- garbage: data bytes before any status, undefined status bytes, a device plugged in mid-stream.

The state is small: the running status byte, the data bytes collected so far, and whether we are inside a SysEx.

```python
# Data lengths for supported System Common.
SYS_LEN = {0xF1: 1, 0xF2: 2, 0xF3: 1}

def data_len(status):
    hi = status & 0xF0
    if hi in (0xC0, 0xD0):
        return 1
    if hi < 0xF0:
        return 2
    return SYS_LEN.get(status, 0)

class Parser:
    def __init__(self):
        self.rs = None      # running status
        self.data = []
        # SysEx content is
        # deliberately discarded.
        self.sysex = False

    def feed(self, b):
        # 1. real-time: act, keep state
        if b in (0xF9, 0xFD):
            return []  # undefined real-time
        if b >= 0xF8:
            return [(b,)]
        # 2. any other status byte
        if b & 0x80:
            self.data = []
            self.sysex = (b == 0xF0)
            if b < 0xF0:       # channel msg
                self.rs = b
            elif b in SYS_LEN:  # sys common
                self.rs = b
            else:               # F0 F4-F7
                self.rs = None
                if b == 0xF6:   # tune req
                    return [(b,)]
            return []
        # 3. data byte
        if self.sysex or self.rs is None:
            return []           # ignore
        # Collect only the
        # required data bytes.
        self.data.append(b)
        need = data_len(self.rs)
        if len(self.data) < need:
            return []
        # Emit only once the
        # message is complete.
        msg = (self.rs, *self.data)
        self.data = []
        if self.rs >= 0xF0:
            self.rs = None  # sys common
        return [msg]

# Print complete messages, not raw byte
# arrival.
def show(stream):
    p = Parser()
    for b in stream:
        for m in p.feed(b):
            print(" ".join(
                f"{x:02X}" for x in m))

show([0x90, 0x3C, 0x64,  # note on
      0x40, 0x64,        # running st.
      0x3C, 0xF8, 0x00,  # clock inside
      0xF2, 0x00, 0x00,  # song pos
      0x3C, 0x00])       # orphan data
```

```output
90 3C 64
90 40 64
F8
90 3C 00
F2 00 00
```

Trace the interesting parts:

1. `40 64` has no status byte; running status reuses `90`, giving a second Note On.
2. `F8` arrives between `3C` and `00`. It is emitted immediately and the half-built Note On survives, so `90 3C 00` still completes (a note off, since velocity is 0).
3. `F2 00 00` is a System Common message (Song Position). System Common **clears** running status, so the final `3C 00` has no status to attach to and is ignored.

This mirrors the receiver rules in the specification's appendix: store the status on channel messages, clear it on System Exclusive and System Common, leave it alone for MIDI real-time messages, and ignore data bytes when there is no status. Undefined System Common bytes (`F4`, `F5`) clear it too, and undefined MIDI real-time bytes (`F9`, `FD`) are simply ignored.

This teaching parser discards SysEx payload rather than implementing patch dumps. Its `rs` field temporarily holds the current System Common status until that message completes; only channel statuses persist across completed messages. Input to `feed` is one actual UART byte, an integer from zero to 255.

The parser emits raw tuples. A separate dispatcher must handle System Reset by resetting synth and parser state to the chosen documented power-up state. Other recognised real-time events do not disturb an unfinished message. The normalisation step turns channel tuples into events your synth understands, and this is where `9n kk 00` becomes a note off and messages for other channels are dropped.

> [!tip] Test the parser on your computer first
> Feed it recorded streams, hand-written edge cases and random bytes. Random input must never crash it or emit a message with a data value above 127. Bugs found here cost seconds; the same bugs found on hardware cost an evening.

## Key takeaways
- Test single-data-byte messages, interrupted messages, SysEx termination and orphan data on the computer.

## Further reading
- [MIDI 1.0 Detailed Specification 4.2.1, including the running status appendix (CCRMA copy)](https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~esteban/teaching/McGill_MUMT306/M1_v4-2-1_MIDI_1-0_Detailed_Specification_96-1-4.pdf)
- [MIDI 1.0 Control Change Messages — MIDI Association](https://midi.org/midi-1-0-control-change-messages)
- [Polyphony and monophony in instruments: note priority — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polyphony_and_monophony_in_instruments)
- [MIDI library for Teensy (serial MIDI) — PJRC](https://www.pjrc.com/teensy/td_libs_MIDI.html)

questions.prompt: The parser receives `C0 05 07`. What should it emit?

options.text: Program Change 5, then ignore `07` as an orphan
options.explanation: Running status applies to all channel voice messages, including Program Change. `07` reuses `C0`.

options.text: A single Program Change with data 5 and 7
options.explanation: Program Change has exactly one data byte, so `05` completes the first message.

options.text: Program Change 5, then Program Change 7
options.explanation: Correct. `C0 05` is complete after one data byte; `07` then uses running status `C0`.

options.text: Nothing until a second data byte for `07` arrives
options.explanation: That would be true only if Program Change had two data bytes. It has one.

questions.workedExample:
1. `C0`: Program Change, channel 1. It needs **one** data byte.
2. `05`: message complete: program 5.
3. `07`: a data byte with running status `C0` still set, so it forms a new Program Change: program 7.

This is why the parser looks up the data length per status. Assuming two bytes for everything would mis-parse this stream.

questions.prompt: A buggy parser assumes every channel message has two data bytes, but correctly restarts an incomplete message on a new channel or System Common status. What happens on `C0 05 90 3C 64`?

options.text: Both messages are applied correctly
options.explanation: The bug changes how `C0 05` is handled: the parser keeps waiting for a second data byte that never arrives.

options.text: It emits Program Change 5 with second byte `90`
options.explanation: `90` is a status byte (bit 7 set), so it can never be used as data.

options.text: The Note On is lost and the program changes to 60
options.explanation: The new status byte resets the parser, so the Note On is intact.

options.text: The Program Change is lost, then the Note On is parsed correctly
options.explanation: Correct. After `05` the parser waits for one more byte; `90` is a status byte that discards the incomplete message, then `90 3C 64` parses normally.

questions.workedExample:
1. `C0 05`: the buggy parser wants two data bytes, so it waits.
2. `90`: a status byte. The spec says a new status byte outside the MIDI real-time class makes the receiver adopt the new status, even if the last message wasn't completed. The half-built Program Change is dropped.
3. `3C 64`: completes Note On key 60.

The symptom ("program changes from the Digitakt sometimes don't work") would be easy to misdiagnose without a unit test for one-data-byte messages.

questions.prompt: The parser receives `F0 7D 01 90 3C 64 F7`. Following the specification, what happens?

options.text: The SysEx is ended by `90`, Note On key 60 plays, and the stray `F7` is ignored
options.explanation: Correct. `90` is a status byte outside the MIDI real-time class, so it terminates the exclusive message. `3C 64` completes the Note On. `F7` then has nothing to end.

options.text: Everything up to `F7` is SysEx data, so no note plays
options.explanation: A SysEx message can be terminated by any status byte except statuses in the System Real-Time class. `90` ends the SysEx.

options.text: The parser should crash or reset because SysEx was malformed
options.explanation: Robust receivers never fail on bad input. The spec explicitly defines how SysEx can be terminated.

options.text: `90` is stored as SysEx data because it follows F0
options.explanation: SysEx data bytes must be 0–127. `90` has bit 7 set, so it is a status byte.

questions.workedExample:
1. `F0`: SysEx starts; running status cleared.
2. `7D 01`: SysEx data (non-commercial ID, then payload).
3. `90`: a status byte. The spec says exclusive messages are terminated by EOX *or any other status byte except statuses in the System Real-Time class*. Note On begins.
4. `3C 64`: Note On key 60, velocity 100.
5. `F7`: End of Exclusive with no open SysEx; ignore it (it also leaves running status cleared).

lessons.title: Track held notes and choose a target
lessons.summary: Track held keys separately from the sounding target, and make priority, retrigger and overflow policies explicit.
lessons.body:
Product details in this unit refer to the original Digitakt OS 1.53 manual and Digitakt II OS 1.17 manual, fetched on 16 October 2026. Confirm your model, firmware and current manual before wiring or configuring it.

## Note priority for a monophonic synth

A mono synth has one voice, but a player (or the Digitakt's chord feature) can hold several keys. The **note priority** rule decides which held key sounds:

- **Last note:** the most recently pressed key wins. Releasing it falls back to the previous one still held. It is one possible policy for a sequenced or keyboard-played monophonic voice.
- **Low note:** the lowest held key wins, whatever order the keys were pressed in.
- **High note:** the highest held key wins.

Which to offer is a design decision; some mono synths let the player choose it as a setting.

The key data structure is a **note stack**: the list of held keys in press order. The rule is applied to the stack after every change.

```python
class MonoVoice:
    def __init__(self, mode="last"):
        self.mode = mode
        self.held = []   # in press order

    def target(self):
        if not self.held:
            return None      # gate off
        if self.mode == "low":
            return min(self.held)
        if self.mode == "high":
            return max(self.held)
        return self.held[-1]  # last

    def note_on(self, n):
        # This policy coalesces
        # repeated keys.
        if n in self.held:
            self.held.remove(n)
        self.held.append(n)
        return self.target()

    # An unheld key is harmless to
    # this policy.
    def note_off(self, n):
        if n in self.held:
            self.held.remove(n)
        return self.target()

events = [("on", 60), ("on", 64),
          ("on", 55), ("off", 55),
          ("off", 64), ("off", 60)]
# Output lists the target after every event.
for mode in ("last", "low", "high"):
    v = MonoVoice(mode)
    out = []
    for kind, n in events:
        f = v.note_on if kind == "on" \
            else v.note_off
        out.append(f(n))
    print(mode, out)
```

```output
last [60, 64, 55, 64, 60, None]
low [60, 60, 55, 60, 60, None]
high [60, 64, 64, 64, 60, None]
```

`None` means no keys are held, so the gate closes and the envelope enters release. This example deliberately keeps one entry per key. Repeated Note Ons for the same channel and key are coalesced, so one Note Off removes that key; this is a simplified monophonic allocation policy, not a universal rule for stacked voices. Transmitters still owe a matching Note Off for every Note On.

Two further design choices:

- **Retrigger or legato.** When the target changes while keys are still held, do you restart the envelope (retrigger) or just glide or jump the pitch (legato)? Many mono synths offer both.
- **Bounded memory.** In firmware the stack is a fixed array (say 16 entries, with oldest-dropping on overflow), never a growing list. Removing a key that isn't in the stack must be harmless.

## Key takeaways
- Track held keys separately from the sounding target, and make priority, retrigger and overflow policies explicit.

lessons.title: Prevent and recover from stuck notes
lessons.summary: Handle both note endings, channel changes and sustain, then provide a panic action for lost events.
lessons.body:
## Stuck notes and how to prevent them

A stuck note is a voice that never receives the note off that should end it. The project brief asks for "no unintended stuck notes", so design against each cause.

| Cause | Defence |
|---|---|
| `9n kk 00` not treated as off | Normalise in the parser |
| Note off on another channel | Track notes per channel |
| Channel changed while held | Release all on change |
| Bytes lost (overflow, unplug) | Count overflows; panic |
| Repeated same-key starts | Choose and document a matching policy |
| Sustain pedal held | Defer offs until pedal up |

**Track held notes, not just "the current note".** If the synth remembers only the sounding note, a note off for an earlier key can be misapplied, or missed entirely. A note stack with a documented repeated-key and sustain policy makes those transitions explicit; it does not by itself guarantee that every MIDI use case is covered.

**Implement the mode messages that silence notes.** In supported Omni-Off operation, All Notes Off (CC 123) releases MIDI-started notes on the applicable channel; the specification says to ignore CC 123 while Omni is on. Channel Mode messages are recognised on the configured Basic Channel, and mode changes 124–127 also have the specified note-release effect. The specification says All Notes Off should send voices into their **release** stage rather than cutting them abruptly. All Sound Off (CC 120) is the hard version: silence as soon as possible. A spec detail worth copying: while the sustain pedal (CC 64) is on, note offs **and** All Notes Off are remembered but not acted on until the pedal is released.

**Don't rely on All Notes Off alone.** The specification says receivers aren't required to recognise it, and transmitters should send individual note offs first. Treat it as a safety net.

**Give yourself a panic action.** A button (or a documented MIDI control instruction) that clears held and sustain-deferred notes, silences or releases voices according to its policy, and resets pitch bend to centre is invaluable during development.

**Consider Active Sensing.** If your source sends `FE` and the receiver supports Active Sensing, a receive-activity timeout should silence its voices and leave Active Sensing mode. The nominal interval is 300 ms; the specification recommends a receiver threshold above 330 ms for margin. This detects missing traffic rather than proving the cable physically came out. If the source never sends `FE`, behave normally.

## Key takeaways
- Handle both note endings, channel changes and sustain, then provide a panic action for lost events.

## Further reading
- [MIDI 1.0 Detailed Specification 4.2.1, including the running status appendix (CCRMA copy)](https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~esteban/teaching/McGill_MUMT306/M1_v4-2-1_MIDI_1-0_Detailed_Specification_96-1-4.pdf)
- [MIDI 1.0 Control Change Messages — MIDI Association](https://midi.org/midi-1-0-control-change-messages)

questions.prompt: Notes from your sequencer occasionally hang until you power-cycle the synth. Which bug would most directly cause this?

options.text: The parser treats Note On with velocity 0 as a new note
options.explanation: Correct. Any transmitter that ends notes with `9n kk 00` will then never end a note, which is a stuck note every time.

options.text: The synth maps CC 74 linearly instead of exponentially
options.explanation: A poor curve affects how the cutoff knob feels; it doesn't stop notes ending.

options.text: The synth ignores Program Change
options.explanation: Ignoring a message type silently is allowed and harmless for note endings.

options.text: The UART is set to 31,250 baud
options.explanation: 31,250 baud is the correct MIDI rate. A wrong rate would garble everything, not just note offs.

questions.workedExample:
1. A stuck note is a voice whose note off is never recognised.
2. Transmitters can end notes with `8n kk vv` or `9n kk 00`, and the spec requires receivers to accept both.
3. If velocity 0 is handled as a note on, every note ended that way will hang.
4. Fix it in the parser's normalisation step, then test with both styles.

questions.prompt: The synth is in Omni-Off mode on Basic Channel 1 and supports All Notes Off and sustain. It receives, in order: `B0 40 7F`, `90 3C 64`, `90 3C 00`, `B0 7B 00`, `B0 40 00`. Following the MIDI specification, when should key 60 enter its release stage?

options.explanation: The sustain pedal (CC 64) is on at this point, so the note off is remembered but not acted on.

options.text: At `B0 7B 00` (All Notes Off)
options.explanation: The spec says sustain also takes priority over All Notes Off until the pedal is released.

options.text: At `B0 40 00` (sustain released)
options.explanation: Correct. With the pedal down, both the note off and All Notes Off are deferred. When the pedal is released, the note is released.

options.text: Never: the note off was lost
options.explanation: It wasn't lost. It is held pending because of the sustain pedal.

questions.workedExample:
```
B0 40 7F  sustain on
90 3C 64  key 60 on
90 3C 00  key 60 off -> deferred
B0 7B 00  All Notes Off -> deferred
B0 40 00  sustain off -> release
```

The spec's appendix states that a sustain-on takes priority over Note Off and All Notes Off until it is released, and that All Notes Off should send voices into their release stage rather than cutting them.

questions.prompt: Which design choices reduce the risk of stuck notes in a MIDI-driven mono synth? Select all that apply.

options.text: Keeping a stack of held keys per channel instead of only the current note
options.explanation: Correct. Tracking held keys per channel gives note offs an explicit target; repeated starts still need a documented allocation/matching policy.

options.text: Releasing all notes when the receive channel is changed in the menu
options.explanation: Correct. Otherwise the matching note offs arrive on the old channel and are ignored.

options.text: Implementing All Notes Off (CC 123) and a panic button
options.explanation: Correct. These are safety nets for when note offs really are lost.

options.text: Ignoring Note Off messages and relying on All Notes Off
options.explanation: Receivers aren't required to recognise All Notes Off, and transmitters only send it occasionally. Note offs are the primary mechanism.

options.text: Counting receive-buffer overflows
options.explanation: Correct. A dropped note-off byte is a future stuck note. The counter shows whether the buffer is too small.

questions.workedExample:
Work through each failure path:

1. Misapplied offs → track held keys (note stack).
2. Offs on the wrong channel → release everything when the channel changes.
3. Offs never received (unplugged cable, overflow) → All Notes Off, Active Sensing, a panic action, and an overflow counter to find the cause.
4. Relying on All Notes Off instead of note offs is backwards: the spec says it should not be used in lieu of note offs.

lessons.title: Map controller steps onto useful ranges
lessons.summary: Choose a curve for the parameter; exponential frequency mapping spreads ratios evenly but does not add MIDI resolution.
lessons.body:
## Mapping CC values to parameters

A CC gives you 0–127. Your synth parameter has a real range and a natural scale. Mapping has three parts.

### 1. Choose the curve

For **frequencies and times**, use an exponential curve, so that equal knob movements give equal musical intervals. The idea: instead of adding a fixed number of hertz per step, *multiply* by a fixed ratio per step, so every step is the same musical interval.

```formula
f = f_lo (f_hi / f_lo)^{v / 127}
f = 20 Hz × (20000 / 20)^{64 / 127}
f ≈ 20 Hz × 1000^{0.504}
f ≈ 649.9 Hz
where
f: the parameter value the knob position maps to, here a filter cutoff in hertz (Hz)
f_lo: the value at CC 0, the bottom of the range; 20 Hz here
f_hi: the value at CC 127, the top of the range; 20,000 Hz (20 kHz) here
v: the received CC value, 0 to 127; 64 is the knob's midpoint
127: the largest CC value, so v / 127 runs from 0 to 1
Hz: hertz, cycles per second
x^{…}: raising to the power in braces
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: the knob's position chooses how far along the ratio from 20 Hz to 20 kHz you are; the midpoint lands near the geometric middle (about 650 Hz), not the arithmetic middle (about 10 kHz).
```

The same mapping in Python, with its values across the knob:

```python
def cc_to_cutoff(v, lo=20.0, hi=20000.0):
    # exponential: equal steps = equal
    # musical intervals
    return lo * (hi / lo) ** (v / 127)

# Output: controller value then cutoff in
# Hz.
for v in (0, 32, 64, 96, 127):
    print(v, round(cc_to_cutoff(v), 1))
```

```output
0 20.0
32 114.0
64 649.9
96 3704.6
127 20000.0
```

Compare a linear map over the same range, which adds a fixed number of hertz per step:

```formula
f = f_lo + ((f_hi − f_lo)v / 127)
f = 20 Hz + 19980 Hz × 1 / 127
f ≈ 177 Hz
where
f: the cutoff the knob position maps to, in hertz (Hz)
f_lo: the value at CC 0; 20 Hz
f_hi: the value at CC 127; 20,000 Hz
v: the CC value; 1 here, the first step above zero
Hz: hertz, cycles per second
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: a linear map adds about 157 Hz per step, which is a huge musical jump at the bottom and an inaudible one at the top.
```

So the step from 0 to 1 jumps from 20 Hz to about 177 Hz (more than three octaves), and half the knob covers 10–20 kHz where little changes audibly. How evenly does the exponential map spread its steps? Count the octaves in the range, then divide them between the 127 steps:

```formula
N_oct = log_2(f_hi / f_lo)
N_oct = log_2(20000 / 20)
N_oct = log_2(1000) ≈ 9.97
Δ = (12 N_oct) / 127
Δ = 12 × 9.97 / 127 ≈ 0.94
where
N_oct: the number of octaves (doublings) between the bottom and top of the range
log_2: logarithm base 2, which counts how many times you must double to get from 1 to the number; log_2(8) = 3
f_hi: the top of the range, 20,000 Hz
f_lo: the bottom of the range, 20 Hz
Δ: the interval covered by one CC step, in semitones (there are 12 semitones in an octave)
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: 20 Hz to 20 kHz is about 10 octaves, or 120 semitones, so 127 equal steps are just under a semitone each.
```

These formulas assume f_lo is above zero (an exponential map can never reach 0 Hz) and that the parameter really is perceived on a ratio scale, as pitch and time are. A linear mapping can suit a control position. A pan control's audible gain law is a separate design choice, so equal position steps need not mean linear channel gains.

A decibel-style curve can be useful for **mix levels**; choose its range and mute behaviour explicitly. For MIDI controllers defined as **switches**, use the documented convention: values up to 63 are off, and values from 64 are on.

## Key takeaways
- Choose a curve for the parameter; exponential frequency mapping spreads ratios evenly but does not add MIDI resolution.

## Further reading
- [MIDI 1.0 Detailed Specification 4.2.1, including the running status appendix (CCRMA copy)](https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~esteban/teaching/McGill_MUMT306/M1_v4-2-1_MIDI_1-0_Detailed_Specification_96-1-4.pdf)
- [MIDI 1.0 Control Change Messages — MIDI Association](https://midi.org/midi-1-0-control-change-messages)
- [Polyphony and monophony in instruments: note priority — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polyphony_and_monophony_in_instruments)
- [MIDI library for Teensy (serial MIDI) — PJRC](https://www.pjrc.com/teensy/td_libs_MIDI.html)

questions.prompt: You map CC 74 (0–127) to filter cutoff between 20 Hz and 20 kHz. Why is an exponential mapping usually better than a linear one?

options.text: Linear mapping cannot reach 20 kHz
options.explanation: Both mappings reach 20 kHz at 127. The difference is how the values are distributed.

options.text: Pitch perception is roughly logarithmic, so equal knob steps should give equal frequency ratios
options.explanation: Correct. Exponential mapping spreads the roughly 10 octaves evenly, at about 0.94 semitones per step. Linear mapping jumps over three octaves in its first step and spends half its range above 10 kHz.

options.text: Exponential mapping removes the need for smoothing
options.explanation: Each step is still a jump of nearly a semitone; smoothing is still needed to avoid zipper noise.

options.text: The MIDI spec requires CC 74 to be exponential
options.explanation: The spec defines CC 74 as Sound Controller 5 (default: brightness). The curve is the receiver's choice.

questions.workedExample:
Compare the low end of each mapping:

Linear mapping:

```formula
f = f_lo + ((f_hi − f_lo)v / 127)
f(1) = 20 Hz + (19980 Hz × 1 / 127)
f(1) ≈ 177 Hz
f(64) = 20 Hz + (19980 Hz × 64 / 127)
f(64) ≈ 10089 Hz
where
f: the cutoff for CC value v, in hertz (Hz); f(1) means the value when v is 1
f_lo: the cutoff at CC 0, 20 Hz
f_hi: the cutoff at CC 127, 20,000 Hz
v: the CC value, 0 to 127
Hz: hertz, cycles per second
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: a linear map adds about 157 Hz per step, so the first step jumps more than three octaves (20 Hz to 177 Hz) and the midpoint is already at 10 kHz.
```

Exponential mapping:

```formula
f = f_lo (f_hi / f_lo)^{v / 127}
f(64) = 20 Hz × 1000^{64 / 127}
f(64) ≈ 650 Hz
N_oct = log_2(1000) ≈ 9.97
Δ = 12 × 9.97 / 127 ≈ 0.94
where
f: the cutoff for CC value v, in hertz (Hz)
f_lo: the cutoff at CC 0, 20 Hz
f_hi: the cutoff at CC 127, 20,000 Hz, so the ratio f_hi / f_lo is 1000
v: the CC value, 0 to 127
N_oct: the number of octaves in the range
log_2: logarithm base 2: how many doublings make the number
Δ: the interval per CC step, in semitones (12 per octave)
Hz: hertz, cycles per second
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: each step multiplies the cutoff by the same ratio, so the 10 octaves are shared evenly at just under a semitone per step.
```

So the whole knob is musically useful with the exponential map.

lessons.title: Smooth control targets in audio
lessons.summary: Publish control targets safely, then smooth them at audio rate using a coefficient matched to the sample rate.
lessons.body:
Product details in this unit refer to the original Digitakt OS 1.53 manual and Digitakt II OS 1.17 manual, fetched on 16 October 2026. Confirm your model, firmware and current manual before wiring or configuring it.

## 2. Use more resolution where it matters


At 128 steps, a slow filter sweep can produce audible stepping. Options: accept 14-bit pairs (each controller from 0 to 31 paired with the controller 32 higher, such as CC 1 with CC 33) where your controller sends them, and in every case **smooth** the value in the audio callback.

### 3. Smooth in the audio domain

The control code only sets a *target*. The audio callback moves the real parameter towards it a little each sample (a one-pole smoother is the usual tool, covered with synthesis DSP). This reduces abrupt control changes and can make zipper noise and MIDI arrival jitter less audible; smoothing adds response lag and cannot guarantee that every modulation artefact vanishes.

Each sample, the smoother closes a fixed fraction of the remaining gap:

```formula
c_new = c + k(c_target − c)
c_new = 1000 Hz + 0.01 × (2000 Hz − 1000 Hz)
c_new = 1010 Hz
where
c_new: the parameter value used for this sample, here a cutoff in hertz (Hz)
c: the value used for the previous sample
c_target: the latest value the control code published from the CC; 2000 Hz in the example
k: the dimensionless smoothing coefficient, strictly between zero and one for a gradual approach; the choice depends on the sample rate and desired smoothing duration
Hz: hertz, cycles per second
In words: every sample, move one small fixed fraction of the way from where the parameter is to where the knob says it should be.
```

For a fixed target and a coefficient strictly between zero and one, each update reduces the remaining gap without overshooting. At zero it never moves; at one it jumps directly to the target. At 48,000 samples per second with a coefficient of 0.01, the gap shrinks to about 37 % of its starting size in about 100 samples, roughly 2 ms. The pseudocode:

```text
control code, on CC 74 value v:
    cutoff_target = cc_to_cutoff(v)
    publish(cutoff_target)   # safe publish

audio callback, per sample:
    cutoff += k * (cutoff_target - cutoff)
    filter.set_cutoff(cutoff)
```

Keep a single **CC map** table in one place: CC number, parameter, curve and range. Print it into your project docs. Use it when configuring the Digitakt MIDI track's CC slots. The publish/read mechanism must be appropriate for the actual platform; this pseudocode does not supply synchronisation.

## Key takeaways
- Publish control targets safely, then smooth them at audio rate using a coefficient matched to the sample rate.

## Further reading
- [One-pole filters — Julius O. Smith](https://www.dsprelated.com/freebooks/filters/One_Pole.html)
- [MIDI 1.0 Detailed Specification 4.2.1, including the running status appendix (CCRMA copy)](https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~esteban/teaching/McGill_MUMT306/M1_v4-2-1_MIDI_1-0_Detailed_Specification_96-1-4.pdf)
- [MIDI 1.0 Control Change Messages — MIDI Association](https://midi.org/midi-1-0-control-change-messages)
- [Polyphony and monophony in instruments: note priority — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polyphony_and_monophony_in_instruments)
- [MIDI library for Teensy (serial MIDI) — PJRC](https://www.pjrc.com/teensy/td_libs_MIDI.html)

questions.prompt: Turning the Digitakt knob mapped to your filter cutoff produces audible stepping (zipper noise). Which changes help? Select all that apply.

options.text: Send the same 7-bit CC more often
options.explanation: More messages carrying the same 128 possible values add no resolution; each change is still a jump.

options.text: Set a target in the control code and smooth towards it in the audio callback
options.explanation: Correct. A sample-by-sample smoother reduces the abrupt control jump and can reduce audible zipper noise; it also introduces response lag.

options.text: Accept 14-bit CC pairs for supported controllers, using the matching controller number 32 higher
options.explanation: Correct. 16,384 steps instead of 128 makes each jump far smaller, though smoothing is still advisable.

options.text: Apply the CC value directly inside the UART interrupt
options.explanation: This makes the jump happen sooner, not more smoothly, and risks races with the audio code.

options.text: Switch from an exponential to a linear cutoff mapping
options.explanation: That makes the low-frequency jumps larger (over three octaves for the first step), not smaller.

questions.workedExample:
1. A 7-bit CC gives 128 discrete values. Each change makes the cutoff jump instantly; those discontinuities are the zipper noise.
2. Smoothing reduces the abrupt change: the control code sets `cutoff_target`, and the audio code moves towards it each sample:

```formula
c_new = c + k(c_target − c)
where
c_new: the cutoff used for this sample, in hertz (Hz)
c: the cutoff used for the previous sample, in hertz
c_target: the latest cutoff the control code published from the CC, in hertz
k: the smoothing coefficient, between 0 and 1; smaller is slower and smoother
Hz: hertz, cycles per second
In words: each sample, close a small fixed fraction of the gap between the current cutoff and the target, so a CC jump becomes a smooth glide.
```

3. More resolution (14-bit pairs) shrinks the jumps at the source.
4. Sending more often, applying sooner, or using a worse curve don't address the cause.

lessons.title: Trace the DIN MIDI current loop
lessons.summary: Check DIN pin numbering from the correct view; current on is logical zero, and MIDI IN keeps its shield free of a DC ground path.
lessons.body:
Product details in this unit refer to the original Digitakt OS 1.53 manual and Digitakt II OS 1.17 manual, fetched on 16 October 2026. Confirm your model, firmware and current manual before wiring or configuring it.

This lesson is about the wires: how a MIDI byte physically gets from the Digitakt to your synth's microcontroller, and why you can't just connect a DIN socket to a GPIO pin. The project's electronics notes say exactly that: "DIN MIDI is not a direct connection to arbitrary GPIO pins." Here is why, and what to build instead.

> [!warning] Low-voltage work only
> Everything in this lesson runs from your development board's 3.3 V or 5 V supply. Never open or modify mains-powered equipment. Before connecting any circuit to a board, check the pin voltage limits in that board's documentation.

## The 5-pin DIN connection

MIDI uses a 5-pin DIN connector with its pins spread over 180°. The MIDI electrical specification (updated in 2014 as document CA-033) fixes the details:

- Devices have **female sockets** labelled MIDI IN, MIDI OUT and (optionally) MIDI THRU. Cables are male-to-male.
- Only **three pins** are used: **pin 4** (current source), **pin 5** (current sink, the data line) and **pin 2** (shield). Pins 1 and 3 are left unconnected.
- The cable is shielded twisted pair, at most **15 m (50 ft)**, with the shield connected to pin 2 at both ends.
- **Pin 2 is grounded at the transmitter only.** At a MIDI IN, pin 2 must have no DC path to the receiver's ground.

That last rule is the key to the whole design, and it comes from how the signal is carried.

## A current loop, not a voltage

Most logic signals are voltages measured against a shared ground. MIDI instead sends a **current of about 5 mA** around a loop through the cable: out of the transmitter on pin 4, through an LED inside the receiver, and back to the transmitter on pin 5.

```diagram
 SENDER                  RECEIVER
 VTX-RA-pin4 ---------> pin4
                         |
                      RB 220
                         |
                     LED anode
                     LED cathode
                         |
 TX--RC-pin5 <--------- pin5
 GND----pin2 --shield-- pin2 (no GND)
```

The current enters the receiver on pin 4 and leaves on pin 5, so the LED's anode faces pin 4. RB and the LED are in series, so it makes no electrical difference which leg RB sits on; follow the reference figure when you build it.

- **Logical 0 = current on.** When the UART's TX pin goes low, current flows from VTX through the loop into TX.
- **Logical 1 = current off.** TX high: no voltage across the loop, no current. The line idles at 1, so an idle UART means no current.

So the UART needs no inversion: start bits (0) light the receiver's LED, stop bits (1) turn it off. The spec also says one output drives exactly one input.

## Key takeaways
- Check DIN pin numbering from the correct view; current on is logical zero, and MIDI IN keeps its shield free of a DC ground path.

## Further reading
- [MIDI 1.0 Electrical Specification Update CA-033 (2014) — MIDI Association](https://www.midi.org/wp-content/uploads/wpforo/default_attachments/1709416667-ca33-MIDI-10-Electrical-Specification-Update.pdf)
- [5 Pin DIN Electrical Specs — MIDI Association](https://midi.org/5-pin-din-electrical-specs)
- [How to make your own 3.5 mm TRS-to-MIDI DIN cables (Type A and B) — MIDI Association](https://midi.org/updated-how-to-make-your-own-3-5mm-mini-stereo-trs-to-midi-5-pin-din-cables)
- [USB Device Class Definition for MIDI Devices 1.0 — USB-IF](https://www.usb.org/sites/default/files/midi10.pdf)
- [USB On-The-Go (host and device roles) — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USB_On-The-Go)
- [Teensy 4.1 (device and host USB ports, 3.3 V pins) — PJRC](https://www.pjrc.com/store/teensy41.html)
- [Opto-isolator — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opto-isolator)

questions.prompt: On a DIN MIDI line, what does the receiver see while the sender's UART is idle (no data)?

options.text: Current flowing continuously, representing logical 1
options.explanation: In MIDI, current ON is logical 0. The idle line is logical 1, so no current flows.

options.text: A 5 V voltage on pin 5 relative to the receiver's ground
options.explanation: The receiver measures current through its LED, not voltages against its own ground; it isn't connected to the sender's ground at all.

options.text: Alternating current at 31.25 kHz
options.explanation: Nothing toggles while idle. Bits only appear when bytes are sent.

options.text: No current in the loop
options.explanation: Correct. The UART idles high (logical 1), so there is no voltage across the loop and the receiver's LED is off.

questions.workedExample:
1. The spec: "The MIDI circuit is a 5mA current loop; logical 0 is current ON."
2. A UART idles at logical 1 (high).
3. With TX high, both ends of the loop sit at about the same potential, so no current flows and the receiver's LED is dark.
4. A start bit (0) pulls TX low, current flows, the LED lights and the receiver's output goes low.

lessons.title: Protect and isolate the MIDI input
lessons.summary: Use the reference isolated input instead of exposing an MCU pin directly to a DIN cable.
lessons.body:
## Why the input needs an optocoupler

The receiver's end of the loop is the LED of an **optocoupler** (opto-isolator): an LED and an electrically isolated light sensor sealed in one package. The only connection between the two sides is light.

This gives **galvanic isolation**:

- The receiver's circuit ground is never connected to the sender's ground through the MIDI cable.
- A correctly isolated DIN MIDI input avoids adding a DC **ground loop** path: a second ground path between two pieces of mains-powered equipment that already share earth through their power leads. Ground loops let current flow in signal grounds, which you hear as hum in audio.
- It separates the receiver logic from the sender's signal voltage, within the component's and circuit's ratings. It is not an unlimited fault or safety-isolation guarantee.

In a studio full of devices connected by audio cables as well as MIDI, this matters. The spec's own words: "To avoid ground loops, and subsequent data errors, the transmitter circuitry and receiver circuitry are internally separated by an opto-isolator."

Wiring the DIN pins straight to a GPIO would tie the grounds together, break this isolation, and expose your microcontroller to whatever the sender drives. With a 3.3 V board whose pins are not 5 V tolerant (PJRC states this for the Teensy 4.1, for example), a 5 V MIDI output could damage it.

## Key takeaways
- Use the reference isolated input instead of exposing an MCU pin directly to a DIN cable.

## Further reading

lessons.summary: Check optocoupler supply, pull-up, speed and pin limits together; an optional shield capacitor preserves DC isolation but is not ideal at every frequency.
lessons.body:
## The reference MIDI IN circuit

Figure 2 of CA-033 gives the input circuit. The essential parts:

| Part | Role |
|---|---|
| RB = 220 Ω | Series resistor in the loop |
| Optocoupler | Isolation; e.g. PC900V, 6N138 |
| D1 (1N914) | Reverse protection for the LED |
| RD (pull-up) | Opto output to VRX |
| Pin 2 | No DC path to ground |

How it works:

1. Loop current flows through RB and the optocoupler's LED.
2. The light detector and output circuitry respond to the LED, pulling the output low against the pull-up RD.
3. That output goes to your UART's RX pin. Current on gives a low (0), current off gives a high (1): the same low/high logic relationship the sender's UART produced.
4. D1, wired across the LED in the reverse direction, stops a reversed or faulty connection from putting a damaging reverse voltage on the LED.

Requirements from the spec: the receiver must need **less than 5 mA** to turn on, and rise and fall times should be under **2 µs**. To see why 2 µs is comfortable, compare it with the length of one bit:

```formula
t_bit = 1 / R
t_bit = 1 bit / (31250 bit/s)
t_bit = 0.000032 s = 32 µs
where
t_bit: the time one bit lasts on the wire, in seconds (s)
R: the DIN MIDI bit rate, 31,250 bits per second (bit/s)
bit: one binary digit
s: seconds
µs: microseconds, millionths of a second
In words: each MIDI bit lasts 32 µs, so a 2 µs edge uses up only about a sixteenth of it.
```

The spec names the Sharp PC900V and Hewlett-Packard 6N138 as acceptable and notes that other high-speed optocouplers may be. Its only recommended RD value is **280 Ω for the PC900V with a 5 V pull-up supply (VRX)**. The reference parts use output circuitry requiring an external pull-up (the 6N138's output pin is the bare collector of its output transistor), which is why the pull-up RD is needed. Acceptance in the older CA-033 example does not prove a part works at a 3.3 V output supply. For a 3.3 V receiver, pick an optocoupler whose actual manufacturer datasheet supports that supply and choose RD from that datasheet. Pull the output up to **your MCU's supply (3.3 V)**, never to 5 V on a pin that isn't 5 V tolerant.

Optional additions in CA-033: ferrite beads on the signal pins, and a **0.1 µF capacitor** from MIDI IN pin 2 (or the jack shield) to ground. A capacitor's opposition to AC (its reactance) falls as frequency rises:

```formula
X_C = 1 / (2πfC)
X_C = 1 / (2 × π × 60 Hz × 0.0000001 F)
X_C ≈ 26500 Ω = 26.5 kΩ
where
X_C: the capacitor's reactance, its opposition to alternating current, in ohms (Ω)
π: pi, about 3.14159
f: the frequency of the signal or interference, in hertz (Hz); 60 Hz here, a mains frequency
C: the capacitance, in farads (F); 0.1 µF = 0.0000001 F
Hz: hertz, cycles per second
F: farad, the unit of capacitance
Ω: ohm, the unit of resistance and reactance
kΩ: kilohm, 1,000 ohms
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: at mains frequencies the 0.1 µF capacitor looks like tens of thousands of ohms, nearly an open circuit.
```

Repeat it at a radio frequency of 10 MHz (10,000,000 Hz) and the reactance is about 0.16 Ω, close to a short circuit. This is the ideal-capacitor approximation used in CA-033, not a complete RF model of a real part or cable. At 20 kHz the same ideal capacitor is about 79.6 Ω, so do not call it an open circuit throughout the audio band. The optional connection preserves DC isolation while giving RF interference a lower-impedance path, as the specification intends.

## Key takeaways
- Check optocoupler supply, pull-up, speed and pin limits together; an optional shield capacitor preserves DC isolation but is not ideal at every frequency.

lessons.summary: Use the resistor values for the specified transmitter voltage and account for receiver and driver drops.
lessons.body:
## The reference MIDI OUT circuit, 3.3 V version

The original 1983 output used +5 V and two 220 Ω resistors. Most current microcontrollers run at 3.3 V, so the 2014 update adds a 3.3 V variant. In Figure 1, RA connects pin 4 to the supply VTX, and RC connects pin 5 to the UART TX (optionally through a buffer):

| VTX | RA (pin 4) | RC (pin 5) |
|---|---|---|
| +5 V ± 10% | 220 Ω 5% 0.25 W | 220 Ω 5% 0.25 W |
| +3.3 V ± 5% | 33 Ω 5% **0.5 W** | 10 Ω 5% 0.25 W |

Pin 2 is grounded at the transmitter. You can check the loop current with Ohm's law, treating the receiver as its 220 Ω RB plus an LED forward voltage drop. All three resistors are in series around the loop, so their resistances add, and the voltage left to push current through them is the supply minus what the LED drops:

```formula
I = (V_TX − V_F) / (R_A + R_C + R_B)
I = (3.3 V − 1.4 V) / (263 Ω)
I = 1.9 V / (263 Ω)
I ≈ 0.00722 A = 7.22 mA
where
I: the loop current, in amperes (A); about 5 mA is the design target
V_TX: the transmitter's supply voltage (VTX), in volts (V); 3.3 V here
V_F: the forward voltage dropped across the optocoupler's LED while it conducts, in volts; typically about 1.4 V to 1.9 V
R_A: the transmitter's resistor from the supply to pin 4, in ohms (Ω); 33 Ω here
R_C: the transmitter's resistor from the UART TX pin to pin 5, in ohms; 10 Ω here
R_B: the receiver's series resistor, 220 Ω
V: volt, the unit of voltage
Ω: ohm, the unit of resistance
A: ampere, the unit of current
mA: milliampere, a thousandth of an ampere
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: the voltage left after the LED's drop, divided by all the resistance in the loop, gives about 7 mA with the 3.3 V resistor values.
```

This ignores the small voltage left across the UART's TX output when it pulls low and the cable's own resistance, which is why the spec quotes ranges rather than one exact figure. The same calculation for all four cases in the spec:

```python
def loop_ma(vtx, ra, rc, vf, rb=220):
    # rb: receiver's series resistor
    # Simplified series loop, no
    # driver drop.
    r = ra + rc + rb
    # Ohm law gives amps; scale to
    # milliamps.
    return (vtx - vf) / r * 1000

# 5 V original circuit, 6N138 Vf 1.7 V
print(round(loop_ma(5.0, 220, 220, 1.7), 2))
# 3.3 V circuit, typical Vf 1.4 V
print(round(loop_ma(3.3, 33, 10, 1.4), 2))
# 3.3 V worst case from CA-033
print(round(loop_ma(3.135, 33*1.05,
                    10*1.05, 1.9,
                    220*1.05), 2))
# mistake: 3.3 V with 5 V resistors
print(round(loop_ma(3.3, 220, 220, 1.4), 2))
```

```output
5.0
7.22
4.47
2.88
```

These match the spec's own figures: 5 mA for the original design, about 7.2 mA typical and 4.47 mA worst case for the 3.3 V design. The last line shows why you mustn't run the 5 V resistor values from 3.3 V: under 3 mA may not reliably switch every receiver.

## Key takeaways
- Use the resistor values for the specified transmitter voltage and account for receiver and driver drops.

lessons.summary: Normal loop current does not determine the worst resistor heating: check the specified electrical short case and driver limits.
lessons.body:
## Why RA is rated 0.5 W
Why is RA rated 0.5 W? If a cable fault shorts pin 4 to ground, RA sits directly across the supply. The spec's worst case is the supply 5% high (3.465 V) and the resistor 5% low (31.35 Ω). Ohm's law gives the current, and the power the resistor must turn into heat follows from the voltage across it:

```formula
I = V / R
I = 3.465 V / (31.35 Ω) ≈ 0.111 A
P = V^2 / R
P = (3.465 V)^2 / (31.35 Ω)
P ≈ 12.006 V^2 / (31.35 Ω)
P ≈ 0.383 W
where
I: the fault current through RA, in amperes (A)
V: the voltage across RA, which during the short is the whole supply, in volts (V); 3.465 V worst case
R: RA's resistance, in ohms (Ω); 33 Ω nominal, 31.35 Ω at −5% tolerance
P: the power dissipated in RA as heat, in watts (W)
A: ampere, the unit of current
Ω: ohm, the unit of resistance
W: watt, the unit of power
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: shorted straight across the supply, the small resistor carries about 111 mA and heats by about 0.38 W, which would overload a 0.25 W part.
```

So the result is about **111 mA and 0.38 W**, below the nominal 0.5 W rating; actual component temperature and derating requirements still matter. The spec also assumes the buffer driving RC in 3.3 V designs is open-collector or open-drain, and warns not to exceed the driving buffer's short-circuit current rating.

> [!tip] Use the published circuit
> Copy CA-033's figures (or your board vendor's documented MIDI circuit) exactly, and note where each value came from. If you use a MIDI breakout or shield, check its schematic against CA-033 for the voltage your board runs at.

## Key takeaways
- Normal loop current does not determine the worst resistor heating: check the specified electrical short case and driver limits.

lessons.title: Choose TRS wiring and plan THRU chains
lessons.summary: Type A puts DIN pin 5 on the tip and pin 4 on the ring; check the actual product, cable and THRU configuration.
lessons.body:
Product details in this unit refer to the original Digitakt OS 1.53 manual and Digitakt II OS 1.17 manual, fetched on 16 October 2026. Confirm your model, firmware and current manual before wiring or configuring it.

## MIDI THRU and daisy chains

A THRU socket re-transmits whatever arrives at IN. Each optocoupler slightly distorts the bit edges, and the errors accumulate along a chain. The spec says that for chains longer than three instruments, faster optocouplers help. Your Digitakt has a THRU port (it can also be set to send DIN sync instead).

## MIDI over TRS minijacks

Small devices often replace the DIN socket with a 3.5 mm TRS (tip-ring-sleeve) jack and an adapter cable. The MIDI Association standardised this in 2018 as **RP-054, which specifies Type A**. RP-054 actually recommends a 2.5 mm TRS connector; its wiring rules also apply when another size such as 3.5 mm is used. Its adapter cable is at most 2 m and uses shielded twisted pair. An ordinary stereo audio cable is not automatically an acceptable direct TRS MIDI cable. Before standardisation, two incompatible wirings spread:

| TRS | Type A (standard) | Type B |
|---|---|---|
| Tip | Pin 5 (sink) | Pin 4 (source) |
| Ring | Pin 4 (source) | Pin 5 (sink) |
| Sleeve | Pin 2 (shield) | Pin 2 (shield) |

The MIDI Association's article (written before RP-054) lists Akai Pro, IK Multimedia, Korg, Line 6, littleBits and Make Noise as using Type A, and Arturia, 1010music and Novation as using Type B. Wiring varies by product, so check each device's manual rather than assuming by brand.

Pins 4 and 5 are swapped between the types, so a Type B adapter on a Type A device drives the loop backwards. The same article says that connecting with incompatible cables "should not damage devices designed in accordance with the MIDI spec": in the reference receiver, the reverse-protection diode D1 conducts instead of the LED, so the loop current stays limited by the resistors, but no data gets through. A device that departs from the reference circuit (for example, one without D1) has no such guarantee. A few devices also use a two-conductor TS jack, sometimes informally called "Type C".

If you put a TRS MIDI jack on your synth, use Type A, label it clearly, and never plug it into an audio jack.

The official RP-054 document also recommends protection against accidental connection to non-MIDI equipment. Follow its reference circuitry rather than inferring safety from connector shape.

## Key takeaways
- Type A puts DIN pin 5 on the tip and pin 4 on the ring; check the actual product, cable and THRU configuration.

lessons.title: Decode USB MIDI 1.0 event packets
lessons.summary: USB MIDI 1.0 parsed event packets contain a cable/type header and complete MIDI bytes, rather than DIN framing.
lessons.body:
## USB MIDI

USB MIDI carries the same MIDI messages over USB, defined by the USB-IF's **Device Class Definition for MIDI Devices** (release 1.0, 1999). Key facts from that document:

- MIDI is a subclass of the USB **Audio** class. A device that follows it is **class-compliant**: operating systems that include a USB MIDI class driver can use it without a vendor driver.
- Data travels in fixed **32-bit USB-MIDI Event Packets**: a header byte with a 4-bit **cable number** (up to 16 virtual MIDI cables per endpoint) and a 4-bit **Code Index Number** (the message type), then three MIDI-byte positions, with unused positions filled with zero.
- Each packet normally holds one complete message, status byte included, so running status isn't used. (The spec also has a single-byte mode, CIN 0xF, for passing an unparsed byte stream, but that is a special case.)

The header byte puts the cable number in its top nibble and the Code Index Number in its bottom nibble:

```formula
H = (n_cable << 4) | CIN
H = (0 << 4) | 0x9 = 0x09
where
H: the packet's header byte, in hexadecimal
n_cable: the virtual cable number, 0 to 15
CIN: the Code Index Number, 0x0 to 0xF; for channel messages it equals the status byte's top nibble (0x9 for Note On, 0xB for Control Change)
<<: bitwise left shift by the given number of bits; a shift of 4 multiplies by 16, moving the cable number into the top nibble
|: bitwise OR, combining the two nibbles
0x: prefix meaning hexadecimal (base 16)
In words: the header is the cable number times 16 plus the message's code index; cable 0 with a Note On gives 0x09.
```

```
Note On, cable 0, ch 1, key 60, vel 100:
09 90 3C 64
^^ cable 0, CIN 9 (note on)
```

A SysEx message can span multiple USB-MIDI Event Packets. Its packet codes distinguish the start/continuation and the final one, two or three bytes; do not assume a whole patch dump fits in one packet.

USB is also much faster than 31,250 bit/s, which helps with dense data. (USB MIDI 2.0, a later class specification, carries MIDI 2.0's packets natively and can fall back to USB MIDI 1.0.)

## Key takeaways
- USB MIDI 1.0 parsed event packets contain a cable/type header and complete MIDI bytes, rather than DIN framing.

## Further reading
- [MIDI 1.0 Electrical Specification Update CA-033 (2014) — MIDI Association](https://www.midi.org/wp-content/uploads/wpforo/default_attachments/1709416667-ca33-MIDI-10-Electrical-Specification-Update.pdf)
- [5 Pin DIN Electrical Specs — MIDI Association](https://midi.org/5-pin-din-electrical-specs)
- [How to make your own 3.5 mm TRS-to-MIDI DIN cables (Type A and B) — MIDI Association](https://midi.org/updated-how-to-make-your-own-3-5mm-mini-stereo-trs-to-midi-5-pin-din-cables)

- [Teensy 4.1 (device and host USB ports, 3.3 V pins) — PJRC](https://www.pjrc.com/store/teensy41.html)
- [Opto-isolator — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opto-isolator)

options.explanation: That is the DIN byte stream. USB MIDI adds a header byte to make a 32-bit packet.
The header comes first, and its high nibble is the cable number.
Correct. The header holds cable 0 in its high nibble and Code Index Number 0xB (Control Change) in its low nibble, followed by the three MIDI bytes.
The status byte is still sent inside the packet. Running status isn't used in parsed USB-MIDI event packets.

1. USB-MIDI Event Packet = 4 bytes: header, then MIDI_0, MIDI_1, MIDI_2.
2. Header = Cable Number (4 bits) followed by Code Index Number (4 bits).
3. Build the header:

```formula
H = (n_cable << 4) | CIN
H = (0 << 4) | 0xB = 0x0B
where
H: the header byte, in hexadecimal
n_cable: the virtual cable number, 0 to 15; 0 here
CIN: the Code Index Number; 0xB for Control Change
<<: bitwise left shift; by 4 bits moves the cable number into the top nibble
|: bitwise OR, combining the two nibbles
0x: prefix meaning hexadecimal (base 16)
In words: cable 0 in the top nibble and code 0xB in the bottom nibble give the header 0x0B.
```
4. MIDI bytes: `B0` (CC, ch 1), `4A` (74), `50` (80).

```
0B B0 4A 50
```

The spec's own example: a CC on cable 10 is `AB Bn pp vv`.

lessons.title: Provide a USB host for MIDI devices
lessons.summary: A device connector does not provide a host; choose DIN or an explicitly supported host and routing arrangement.
lessons.body:
Product details in this unit refer to the original Digitakt OS 1.53 manual and Digitakt II OS 1.17 manual, fetched on 16 October 2026. Confirm your model, firmware and current manual before wiring or configuring it.

## Host and device: why two USB gadgets can't talk

USB is not peer-to-peer. Every USB connection has exactly one **host**, which schedules all transfers, and one or more **devices**, which only respond when the host polls them. Devices cannot talk to each other except via the host, and two hosts can't talk over USB directly. (USB On-The-Go and dual-role ports can switch roles, one end must provide a supported host role; the other can be an ordinary USB device.)

What this means for your setup:

- Both Digitakt models have a USB-B socket for connecting to a computer host, so the Digitakt acts as a USB **device**.
- Most development boards' main USB port is also a **device** port.
- Plug a USB-device synth into a USB-device Digitakt and **nothing happens**: there is no host. A matching cable shape doesn't mean the connection can work.

Ways to connect two USB devices:

1. **A computer as host.** Both plug into the computer, and software (Ableton, or a MIDI routing utility) forwards messages between them.
2. **A board with a USB host port.** PJRC's Teensy 4.1, for example, has a second USB port that operates in host mode, separate from its device port, supported by the USBHost_t36 library.
3. **A standalone USB MIDI host box** that hosts both devices and forwards between them.
4. **Use DIN MIDI instead.** Point to point, isolated, no host needed. For the illustrated standalone link, DIN avoids the USB host requirement; the final interface remains a project decision.

> [!note] Ordinary USB adds a ground path
> An ordinary non-isolated USB implementation joins host and device grounds. A product with an isolated USB implementation is an exception; do not infer its internal ground paths just from the connector. DIN MIDI doesn't, because of the optocoupler. That is one reason USB connections between mains-powered studio gear can introduce hum, as **Diagnose ground paths and run a test session** discusses. (Elektron lists the original Digitakt's USB port as electrically isolated; check your own model's documentation.)

## Key takeaways
- A device connector does not provide a host; choose DIN or an explicitly supported host and routing arrangement.

lessons.title: Choose the right audio input
lessons.summary: Match signal level and load requirements from documentation before connecting outputs to inputs.
lessons.body:
MIDI tells your synth what to play. This lesson is about the other cable: the **audio** that leaves your synth and goes into the audio interface. Getting it wrong gives you noise, hum, distortion, a quiet signal or, at worst, damaged equipment. Getting it right is mostly a matter of knowing the level conventions and a few circuit principles.

> [!warning] Safety boundaries
> Everything here concerns low-voltage signal connections. Don't open mains-powered gear, and never "fix" hum by removing a mains earth. Before connecting a home-built circuit to the interface, check the interface manual's maximum input level and connect with the gain turned down.

## The level hierarchy

Audio connections come in families with very different voltages and impedances:

| Level | Typical source | Goes into |
|---|---|---|
| Mic | Microphone | Mic preamp |
| Instrument | Guitar pickup | Hi-Z input |
| Line | Synth, mixer, DAC | Line input |
| Headphone | Headphone amp | Headphones |
| Speaker | Power amplifier | Passive speaker |

- **Mic level** is weak and varies widely between microphones (it is sometimes quoted as around −60 dBV). The required preamp gain depends on the microphone, source and distance; this quoted level is an illustration, not a fixed mic-level standard.
- **Passive-pickup output** comes from sources like guitar pickups that can supply very little current. "Hi-Z" instrument inputs present a high input impedance chosen for the pickup; consult the instrument and interface documentation so as not to load them.
- **Line level** is the level synths, mixers and interfaces use between each other. It is where your synth's output belongs.
- **Headphone outputs** are amplifiers designed for a specified range of headphone loads; check the supported impedance and output ratings.
- **Speaker level** outputs from power amplifiers drive passive loudspeakers (usually 4–8 Ω) with much higher voltages and currents.

These are **not interchangeable**. A speaker output into a line input can overload or damage it. A line output into a speaker is nearly a short circuit for the line driver: very weak sound and a possibly damaged output. A headphone output can sometimes feed a line input with a suitable stereo-to-mono breakout and conservative level, but check both manuals: a stereo headphone TRS output is not balanced mono, and its peak voltage can overload an input.

## Key takeaways
- Match signal level and load requirements from documentation before connecting outputs to inputs.

lessons.title: Convert between line levels and volts
lessons.summary: Compare dBu and dBV through their level reference voltages; their displayed numbers cannot be subtracted directly.
lessons.body:
## Decibels with a reference: dBV and dBu

A decibel figure is a ratio. To describe an absolute voltage it needs a reference:

- **dBV**: relative to **1 V RMS**.
- **dBu**: relative to **0.7746 V RMS**, a holdover from 600 Ω telephone practice: the voltage that dissipates 1 mW in 600 Ω.

Where does 0.7746 V come from? Power in a resistor is voltage squared divided by resistance, so the voltage that gives a chosen power is the square root of power times resistance:

```formula
V_u = √(PR)
V_u = √(0.001 W × 600 Ω)
V_u = √(0.6) V ≈ 0.7746 V
where
V_u: the dBu level reference voltage (0 dBu), RMS, in volts (V)
P: the reference power, 1 milliwatt = 0.001 watts (W)
R: the reference load, 600 ohms (Ω), the old telephone-line standard
√: square root
W: watt, the unit of power
Ω: ohm, the unit of resistance
V: volt, the unit of voltage
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: 0.7746 V RMS is the voltage that would deliver one milliwatt into 600 ohms.
```

Today the 600 Ω load is history: 0 dBu just means 0.7746 V RMS, whatever the actual load.

To turn a level in decibels into a voltage, undo the decibel formula for voltage ratios (which uses 20 times the base-10 logarithm):

```formula
V_L = V_ref 10^{L / 20}
V_L = 0.7746 V × 10^{4 / 20}
V_L = 0.7746 V × 1.585 ≈ 1.228 V
where
V_L: the RMS voltage the level L describes, in volts (V)
V_ref: the level reference voltage: 0.7746 V for dBu, 1 V for dBV
L: the level in decibels relative to that reference (dBu or dBV); +4 here
10^{…}: 10 raised to the power in braces; it undoes a base-10 logarithm
V: volt, the unit of voltage
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: every 20 dB multiplies the voltage by 10, so +4 dB is about 1.585 times the reference, and +4 dBu is about 1.228 V RMS.
```

For −10 dBV the same formula, with a 1 V reference and a power of −10/20, gives about 0.316 V. The two nominal line levels:

- **Professional: +4 dBu.**
- **Consumer: −10 dBV.**

To compare two voltages in decibels, go the other way:

```formula
ΔL = 20 log_10(V_1 / V_2)
ΔL = 20 log_10(1.228 V / 0.316 V)
ΔL = 20 log_10(3.88) ≈ 11.8 dB
where
ΔL: the difference in level, in decibels (dB); Δ (delta) means "difference"
log_10: the base-10 logarithm: the power you raise 10 to in order to get the number; log_10(100) = 2
V_1: the larger voltage, RMS; 1.228 V (+4 dBu)
V_2: the smaller voltage, RMS; 0.316 V (−10 dBV)
V: volt
dB: decibel
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: pro line level is about 3.9 times the voltage of consumer line level, which is about 11.8 dB.
```

You can't just subtract −10 from +4 to get 14 dB, because the two figures use different references (0.7746 V and 1 V); converting both to volts first avoids that trap. The same sums in Python:

```python
import math

# Historical reference: 1 mW into 600 ohms.
DBU_REF = math.sqrt(0.6)   # 0.7746 V
DBV_REF = 1.0

def dbu_to_v(dbu):
    return DBU_REF * 10 ** (dbu / 20)

def dbv_to_v(dbv):
    return DBV_REF * 10 ** (dbv / 20)

# Voltages are RMS; peak below assumes a
# sine.
pro = dbu_to_v(4)
con = dbv_to_v(-10)
print(f"+4 dBu  = {pro:.3f} V rms")
print(f"-10 dBV = {con:.3f} V rms")
print(f"peak    = {pro*math.sqrt(2):.3f} V,"
      f" {con*math.sqrt(2):.3f} V")
print(f"gap     = "
      f"{20*math.log10(pro/con):.2f} dB")
```

```output
+4 dBu  = 1.228 V rms
-10 dBV = 0.316 V rms
peak    = 1.736 V, 0.447 V
gap     = 11.78 dB
```

For a pure sine, peak voltage is about 1.414 times RMS voltage; that relationship explains the peak output line above. The following headroom unit explains why it does not hold for an arbitrary waveform.

## Key takeaways
- Compare dBu and dBV through their level reference voltages; their displayed numbers cannot be subtracted directly.

```formula
where
V_L: the RMS voltage at level L, in volts (V)
V_ref: the dBu reference, 0.7746 V RMS (the square root of 0.6)
L: the level in dBu; +4 here
10^{…}: 10 raised to the power in braces
V_peak: the peak voltage of a sine wave at that RMS level
√2: the square root of 2, about 1.414
V: volt
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: +4 dB is a voltage ratio of about 1.585, so +4 dBu is about 1.228 V RMS, and a sine at that level peaks at about 1.74 V.
```

The 0.7746 V reference is the voltage that dissipates 1 mW in 600 Ω, a holdover from telephone practice.

questions.prompt: How many decibels higher is professional +4 dBu than consumer −10 dBV?

options.text: About 11.8 dB
options.explanation: Correct. 1.228 V is about 3.88 times 0.316 V, and a voltage ratio of 3.88 is about 11.8 dB.

options.text: 14 dB, because 4 − (−10) = 14
options.explanation: The two figures use different references (0.7746 V and 1 V), so you can't subtract them directly.

options.text: About 6 dB

options.text: They are the same level expressed differently

questions.workedExample:

```formula
V_L = V_ref 10^{L / 20}
V_pro = 0.7746 V × 10^{4 / 20}
V_pro ≈ 1.228 V
V_con = 1 V × 10^{−10 / 20}
V_con ≈ 0.316 V
where
V_L: the RMS voltage at a level L, in volts (V)
V_ref: the level reference voltage: 0.7746 V for dBu, 1 V for dBV
L: the level in decibels relative to that reference
V_pro: the RMS voltage of +4 dBu
V_con: the RMS voltage of −10 dBV
10^{…}: 10 raised to the power in braces
V: volt
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: convert each level to volts using its own reference.
```

2. Compare the two voltages in decibels:

```formula
ΔL = 20 log_10(V_pro / V_con)
ΔL = 20 log_10(1.228 V / 0.316 V)
ΔL = 20 log_10(3.88) ≈ 11.8 dB
where

V_con: 0.316 V RMS (−10 dBV)

dB: decibel
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)

```

The naive 14 dB answer misses the difference between the references: 1 V is about 2.2 dB above 0.7746 V.

lessons.title: Distinguish RMS, peaks and headroom
lessons.summary: Use the square-root-of-two factor only for a sine wave and leave room above the nominal operating level.
lessons.body:
Product details in this unit refer to the original Digitakt OS 1.53 manual and Digitakt II OS 1.17 manual, fetched on 16 October 2026. Confirm your model, firmware and current manual before wiring or configuring it.

## Sine-wave peaks and operating level
So pro line level is about four times the voltage of consumer line level, about 12 dB higher. The "peak" line uses the relationship between a sine wave's RMS value and its peak:

```formula
V_peak = V_rms √2
V_peak = 1.228 V × 1.414
V_peak ≈ 1.736 V
where
V_peak: the highest voltage the sine wave reaches, measured from 0 V, in volts (V)
V_rms: the RMS (root mean square) voltage, the "effective" value that level figures quote, in volts
√2: the square root of 2, about 1.414
V: volt
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: a sine wave's peaks are about 1.41 times its RMS value, so +4 dBu (1.228 V RMS) swings to about ±1.74 V.
```

The factor of about 1.414 holds only for a pure sine wave. Other waveforms and music can have a different, including higher, ratio of peak to RMS, which is one reason equipment needs headroom.

Two cautions:

- **Nominal is not maximum.** The nominal level is the design's operating level; real signals have peaks well above it, and equipment leaves **headroom** for them. Elektron, for example, specifies the Digitakt II's main outputs and inputs at +18 dBu peak, and the original Digitakt's main outputs at +22 dBu peak. Analogue-to-digital alignment is equipment-dependent; −18 and −20 dBFS are examples used in some systems, not a universal correspondence to a particular dBu voltage.
- **Interfaces differ.** Many line inputs are switchable or have enough gain range to handle both conventions. Read your interface manual for its *maximum* input level (often in dBu) and compare it with your synth's maximum output.

Elektron labels these published maximum ratings “dBu peak”. The standard dBu voltage reference is RMS-based; the manufacturer label is quoted here rather than silently converted into waveform peak volts. Confirm the test/measurement convention and permitted input voltage when comparing equipment.

## Key takeaways
- Use the square-root-of-two factor only for a sine wave and leave room above the nominal operating level.

2. A sine wave has a peak about 1.414 times its RMS value; a symmetric square wave has equal peak magnitude and RMS.
3. Other waveforms can place short peaks higher still, so leave headroom and inspect the actual waveform instead of applying the sine-only factor universally.

lessons.title: Check the output and input impedances
lessons.summary: Model the resistive divider, then check the real output driver’s load and current ratings rather than extrapolating beyond them.
lessons.body:
Product details in this unit refer to the original Digitakt OS 1.53 manual and Digitakt II OS 1.17 manual, fetched on 16 October 2026. Confirm your model, firmware and current manual before wiring or configuring it.

## Impedance bridging

Audio line connections are not impedance-*matched* (that is for power transfer and radio). They use **impedance bridging**: a **low output impedance** drives a **high input impedance**. A line driver is normally specified for a minimum load impedance; the receiver should present a much higher impedance than the source. These are design and product specifications, not fixed universal values.

In this resistive Thevenin model, the output and input impedances form a voltage divider: the source's voltage is shared between its own output impedance and the input impedance in proportion to their sizes, and only the input's share reaches the next stage.

```formula
V_in = (V_src Z_in) / (Z_out + Z_in)
V_in = (1 V × 10000 Ω) / (10440 Ω)
V_in = 1 V × 0.958 ≈ 0.958 V
where
V_in: the voltage that actually arrives at the input, in volts (V)
V_src: the voltage the source generates internally, before its own output impedance, in volts
Z_in: the input impedance of the receiving device, in ohms (Ω); 10 kΩ here
Z_out: the output impedance of the source, in ohms; 440 Ω here (Elektron's figure for the Digitakt)
V: volt
Ω: ohm, the unit of resistance and impedance
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: the bigger the input impedance compared with the output impedance, the closer the received voltage is to the full source voltage.
```

In decibels a voltage ratio of 0.958 is about −0.4 dB, a negligible loss. The Digitakt's main outputs have a 440 Ω output impedance (Elektron's figure, unbalanced). See what happens to a 1 V signal from a 440 Ω source as the load changes:

```python
def bridged(v_src, z_out, z_in):
    # output and input form a divider
    return v_src * z_in / (z_out + z_in)

import math
# These are ideal resistive load examples.
for z_in in (10_000, 1_000, 32, 8):
    v = bridged(1.0, 440, z_in)
    # The source is 1 V, so v is also
    # the ratio.
    db = 20 * math.log10(v)
    print(f"{z_in:>6} ohm: {v:.3f} V"
          f" ({db:.1f} dB)")
```

```output
 10000 ohm: 0.958 V (-0.4 dB)
  1000 ohm: 0.694 V (-3.2 dB)
    32 ohm: 0.068 V (-23.4 dB)
     8 ohm: 0.018 V (-35.0 dB)
```

Into a 10 kΩ line input, almost nothing is lost. Into a 32 Ω headphone or 8 Ω speaker, nearly all the voltage is dropped inside the source, and the output stage is asked for far more current than it was designed for. That is the numerical reason line, headphone and speaker connections are not interchangeable.

The calculations are a linear resistive model, not proof that a real driver remains linear into headphones or a speaker. Outside its rated load it can limit current, distort, overheat or become unstable. Design the synth output for the actual receiving input and follow the buffer or codec driver's documented minimum load.

## Key takeaways
- Model the resistive divider, then check the real output driver’s load and current ratings rather than extrapolating beyond them.

options.text: About 0.4 dB
options.explanation: Correct. 10,000 / 10,440 ≈ 0.958, which is −0.37 dB: negligible. This is impedance bridging working as intended.

options.text: About 6 dB, because impedances should be matched
options.explanation: Matching (equal impedances) would lose 6 dB. Audio line connections deliberately bridge instead.

options.text: About 3.2 dB
options.explanation: That would be the loss into a 1 kΩ load, which is much lower than a typical line input.

options.text: Nothing at all
options.explanation: There is a small divider loss, but it is under half a decibel.

questions.workedExample:
```formula
V_in / V_src = Z_in / (Z_out + Z_in)
V_in / V_src = 10000 Ω / 10440 Ω
V_in / V_src ≈ 0.958
ΔL = 20 log_10(0.958) ≈ −0.37 dB
where
V_in: the voltage arriving at the input, in volts
V_src: the voltage the source generates before its output impedance, in volts
Z_in: the input impedance, 10,000 ohms (Ω)
Z_out: the source's output impedance, 440 Ω
ΔL: the change in level, in decibels (dB); negative means a loss
log_10: the base-10 logarithm
Ω: ohm, the unit of impedance
dB: decibel
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: the input receives about 96% of the source voltage, a loss of under half a decibel.
```

A low output impedance into a high input impedance (roughly 20× or more here) passes almost all the voltage and draws little current.

questions.prompt: Why shouldn't you connect a line output directly to an 8 Ω passive speaker?

options.text: The speaker would be damaged by the line output's high voltage
options.explanation: Line outputs have low voltage and little current capability; the risk is to the line output, not the speaker.

options.text: Speakers need a balanced connection
options.explanation: Passive speakers are driven by amplifier outputs; balance isn't the issue.

options.text: It works fine, just slightly quieter
options.explanation: The resistive example predicts a loss of about 35 dB, and a real line driver may distort or limit current outside its rated load. This is not a suitable loudspeaker connection.

options.text: The 8 Ω load is nearly a short circuit for the line driver: the sound is very weak and the output may be damaged
options.explanation: Correct. Line outputs are designed for loads around 10 kΩ; 8 Ω is about a thousand times lower.

questions.workedExample:
1. Work out the voltage divider with a 440 Ω source and an 8 Ω load:

```formula
V_in / V_src = Z_in / (Z_out + Z_in)
V_in / V_src = 8 Ω / 448 Ω ≈ 0.018
ΔL = 20 log_10(0.018) ≈ −35 dB
where
V_in: the voltage reaching the speaker
V_src: the voltage the line output generates internally
Z_in: the load impedance, the 8 Ω speaker
Z_out: the line output's impedance, 440 Ω
ΔL: the change in level, in decibels (dB)
log_10: the base-10 logarithm
Ω: ohm, the unit of impedance
dB: decibel
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: under 2% of the voltage reaches the speaker; the rest is lost inside the source.
```

2. A real driver may current-limit, distort or overheat outside its load rating; the divider model alone does not predict which occurs.
3. A power amplifier is designed for this: high current into 4–8 Ω.
4. Lesson: line, headphone and speaker connections aren't interchangeable.

lessons.title: Read balanced and stereo jack wiring
lessons.summary: A balanced line relies on impedance symmetry and a differential receiver; a TRS connector alone proves neither balance nor signal type.
lessons.body:
Product details in this unit refer to the original Digitakt OS 1.53 manual and Digitakt II OS 1.17 manual, fetched on 16 October 2026. Confirm your model, firmware and current manual before wiring or configuring it.

## Balanced and unbalanced connections

An **unbalanced connection** uses two conductors: signal and ground (which is also the shield). Any noise induced onto the signal wire, or any voltage difference between the two devices' grounds, adds directly to the audio.

A **balanced connection** (a **balanced line**) uses three: two signal conductors (hot and cold) with **equal impedances to ground**, plus a shield. Interference couples almost equally onto hot and cold, so much of it appears as a **common-mode** voltage. A differential receiver responds primarily to the **difference** between the conductors. Rejection is finite and depends on impedance balance, cable construction and the receiver.

Notes that save confusion:

- Balancing is about **equal impedances**, not necessarily equal and opposite signals. An "impedance-balanced" output that drives only the hot leg, with the cold leg tied to ground through a matching impedance, can still provide common-mode rejection with a suitable balanced receiver. Elektron describes the Digitakt's main outputs as impedance balanced.
- Balanced connections usually use **XLR** or **1/4″ TRS**: tip = hot, ring = cold, sleeve = ground and shield.
- The same TRS plug is also used for **unbalanced stereo** (headphones: tip = left, ring = right). The connector alone doesn't tell you which; the jack's documentation does.
- **TS** (tip-sleeve) plugs are unbalanced mono.

Mixing them: a TS plug in a balanced output usually shorts the cold leg to ground. That is normal and fine for impedance-balanced outputs, but for some output designs the cold leg should be left disconnected instead, so check the manual. An unbalanced source can feed a balanced input using the manufacturer's recommended wiring. Noise rejection depends on the resulting impedances and connections; do not assume a particular amount of rejection survives or is lost.

> [!tip] For your first build
> An unbalanced mono output on a 1/4″ TS jack, buffered to a low output impedance, into a balanced line input on your interface, using a short cable, is a perfectly good start. Balanced output stages can come later if hum or noise demands it.

## Key takeaways
- A balanced line relies on impedance symmetry and a differential receiver; a TRS connector alone proves neither balance nor signal type.

questions.prompt: How does a balanced connection reject interference picked up along a cable?

options.text: The shield blocks all interference before it reaches the conductors
options.explanation: The shield helps, but the defining mechanism of balanced audio is common-mode rejection at the receiver.

options.text: The signal is sent at a higher voltage, so interference is relatively smaller
options.explanation: A higher signal voltage is not what defines balance. Noise rejection depends on impedance balance, cable construction and the receiving circuit.

options.text: Interference appears almost equally on hot and cold (common mode), and the receiver amplifies only their difference
options.explanation: Correct in the balanced-line model. Symmetric impedances and suitable cabling make interference predominantly common mode; the differential input rejects it to the extent of its finite common-mode rejection.
